The gown followed behind in the arms of her apprentice, wrapped in muslin like a body prepared for burial, and Margaret directed them through the house with the voice she kept for footmen and bad news.

“On the stand, by the window. Mind the hem. Elara, stand away from the light so we can see the silk.”

Elara stepped back until the bed met her knees. Margaret drew the drapes wide without asking, letting in a sheet of pale light that fell exactly where the dress would stand. Choreography. Her mother had always possessed a genius for it.

The apprentice unwrapped the muslin, and the silk came out like a held breath let go. White. That was all it truly was—white, worked to a heavy liquid quality that swallowed the light, with lace at the throat and wrists and a train that pooled on the floor like moonlight. Vexford had sent money for it. Elara thought of that as Mistress Peveril shook out the folds: a cold-eyed man two days east, spending silver on silk for a woman he had measured like a mare. She had seen the accounts list that traveled with his first letter—columns of economy, of heirs, of a household to be run under his hand. The dress was not a gift. It was a uniform, tailored to a shape she no longer filled.

“Stand, my lady.”

She stood. The shift beneath was thin, and the room kept a turned-back edge of cold; gooseflesh rose along her arms as the gown went over her head. It slid down her body, settled over her chest like a palm laid flat, and waited. The lining was smooth and cool, a second skin with a temperature of its own. Mistress Peveril gathered the excess at Elara’s waist and made a small noise at the back of her throat.

“She has grown thinner than the measuring.”

“Grief ran through her,” Margaret said from the window seat, where the estate correspondence lay like a patient she was diagnosing. “But she has recovered. Haven’t you, Elara?”

“Yes, Mother.” The words answered before she could think. A reflex, like the curtsey her hand made when the door opened.

“It will be taken in,” Mistress Peveril murmured, kneading the cloth at Elara’s waist. “I will recall the curves.”

*I will recall the curves.* As if a body were a debt that could be reimbursed. The seamstress’s fingers were quick and impersonal—ribs, collarbone, the sharp shelf of her shoulders—mapping the places the hollow days had planed away. Elara had eaten since. Bread from Bess’s hand, honeycomb, cheese; the strength had returned to her legs. But the dress knew better. It took the full measure of what she had become to survive, and it would be pulled tight to that shape, and they would all call it lovely.

Margaret rose and came close, her voice taking on the soft carrying quality she used when the servants were within earshot and the truth required a curtain. She touched the lace at Elara’s throat, arranging it, and her rose water bloomed in the warm air.

“This is not what I had. I married for land, because my father was impatient and there was no better offer. Your father’s name is old, but the house—you see the house. I have spent twenty years making it look hale, and it has cost me. Do not think I resent the cost. It was mine to pay. But you will have both.” She smoothed the lace down: a collar being shown to a dog before buckling. “The title and the lands. Blackmoor and the Vexford fortune. Your children will carry a name that opens doors before they have to knock.”

The scream rose then, from no warning, filling the space behind Elara’s tongue like a fish sliding up from deep water. All she had to do was open her lips. *I am in love with a stable hand. He is alive or dead on the moors and I do not know which, and it does not matter, because I am going anyway.* She did not open her lips. She dropped the harbor names into the well of her silence, one by one: *Coldwell. Blackwater. Saltcombe. Rook’s Reach.* She had taught herself to do this in the hollow days, when food would not go down the same throat and the silence had a voice of its own. The names were a rope. She pulled herself up on it.

“Tell me, Mother,” her mouth said, in the tone she had practiced until it passed for obedience, “will Lord Vexford’s tenants be pleased to meet his bride?”

“The tenants will know their place.” It was quoted, and beneath it Elara heard Vexford’s dinner voice—*the lash comes before the eviction*—and her mother’s bright, brittle laugh agreeing with him. Margaret had said the world would hear only that a serving man stole from the chapel. She had said fevers pass.

*We are all fools in youth,* Margaret had told her once, in the very room where Kael’s story had been buried alive. *There was a fate I barely escaped.* Elara looked at her mother’s face, at the lines cream could not soften, and asked, flatly: “Were you ever afraid?”

Margaret’s hand dropped. Something crossed her face—some old, private thing, a door opening on a corridor Elara had never been allowed to walk. For two heartbeats she saw the girl her mother had been: a young woman at a locked window with a moonless night waiting, and a name she had trained herself not to say. Then Margaret smiled the painted-on smile she had worn at Vexford’s dinner, and the door closed again.

“Every bride is afraid. And every bride discovers that fear was a luxury she could not afford. Now hold still while the seamstress pins.”

Mistress Peveril was on her knees, turning up the hem. Elara looked at her reflection in the washstand mirror. A ghost. The white had turned her skin gray; her collarbones stood out beneath the lace like a ledge over a drop. The gown had been cut for a fuller woman, and they would haul it back down to the shape she actually wore, and call her lovely, and send her east, and she would be buried in white or something very like it, and the moors would never know her name.

*You are not here,* she told the reflection. It held no heat. That had frightened her once, in the first days after Kael was cast out. Then she had understood: the cold was useful. It made her precise. She measured the night of her escape the way Mistress Peveril measured her body—in fingers, in lengths, in all the small improvements of attention that make a thing fit at last.

The riding habit was in the bottom drawer of the armoire. Bess had put it there, mended, the seam claimed by a bramble in the herb garden. Elara did not look at the armoire. She let her eyes rest on the window instead, where the gray-green moors ran out in their long, patient roll. Somewhere beyond the glass was the drove road to Coldwell, the track to the shepherd’s wall, the loose stone and the cache beneath it, the ford marked with a cross. And somewhere beyond that was a man with a ruined back walking east, reciting the harbor names to keep himself moving. She did not know if he had found the cache. She did not know if he was alive. She had forced herself to ask the question and found she did not know the answer—and that it did not matter, because she was going anyway.

“Nights,” she said aloud. “Nights—do you have enough pins? There, at the hem. It trails.”

“It is meant to trail, my lady,” the seamstress said, but she turned the hem under anyway, hiding the lie with another lie, and Elara stood perfectly still and let herself be pinned.

A knock. Margaret said *enter* without looking up, and Martha came in. She carried a tray—thread, small scissors, a bowl of water for the seamstress’s hands—and crossed the room with the economy of a woman who had spent twenty-two years making herself unremarkable. She set the tray down, curtseyed, exactly as polite as the occasion required. Then her eyes came up, found Elara’s in the mirror, and held.

Elara wore the white gown. Her shoulders were bare; the lace lay at her throat like a hand on her pulse. The small, settled smile moved at the corner of Martha’s mouth. She said nothing. She did not need to. The smile had a shape: *I have seen you without this dress, and you are no bride to me. You are a woman caught, and I am the one who caught you.*

“Grief passes,” Martha said softly, an echo of her own words from the passage two days ago, and curtseyed a second time, and was gone.

Elara’s hands were fists at her sides. She uncurled them slowly, finger by finger, and heard the names again—stones dropped into a well: *Coldwell. Blackwater. Saltcombe. Rook’s Reach.*

“My lady.” The seamstress’s hands found her ankle. “I must beg you to stand very still. I will pin the last of it.”

The silk lay in a white pool at Elara’s feet. The pins went in one after another, each with a small, decisive push. Elara looked down at the crown of the gray head below her, the black-clad shoulders, the endless white, and thought of the grass bracelet. It was in the pocket of the dressing gown hanging behind the door; she had worked it off when the seamstress asked for her bare arms and hidden it in her fist. Her wrist beneath the lace looked wrong—alien, naked in a way no amount of silk could cover. Kael had braided that bracelet out of dried grass and a strand of his own hair in the hunting lodge, with the rain coming down through the broken roof. *Everything a man makes with his hands breaks,* he had said. *That doesn’t mean he shouldn’t make it.* She carried the saying in her chest now, with the harbor names and the map and the ledger of promises he had made and could not keep—the door, the table, the garden, the shelf for the sea book, the promise to carry her across every river, and the cradle he had deferred and she had let him, the heaviest thing she owned. He had made her a bracelet that would break. She would wear it anyway.

That was the whole of her, standing in a white dress being pinned into someone else’s life.

“Turn, if you please.”

She turned. The mirror gave her to herself again, remade—taken in at waist and sides, the silk clinging to the hollow of her stomach and the sharp drop of her shoulders. It was beautiful, in the way a shroud is beautiful, and Margaret rose from the window seat with her hands clasped beneath her chin.

“Oh,” Margaret said. “Elara. You look precisely as I dreamed they would see you.”

*They will see a dead girl wearing white,* Elara thought, *and I will already be gone.* She smiled at her reflection. It was her mother’s smile, bright and brittle, practiced for the mirror, for the empty door, for the cold-eyed man coming east to collect her. The mask settled. It fit as well as the dress.

Mistress Peveril knelt for the final turn of the hem. Over her bowed head, Elara looked into the long white road of silk running to the floor, and thought of other roads: the passage behind the armoire with its twenty-three black treads, the ninth and the sixteenth and the twentieth that creaked; the stillroom door opening from her side; the latched side door into the herb garden; the gap in the garden wall by the apple trees; the wool cloak under the rosemary bush; the bread, the cheese, the flint and steel, the blade; the riding habit in the bottom drawer; Storm’s warm back and the moonless dark and the long gray road east, with the harbor names on her breath like a song.

The seamstress put the last pin in.

“There,” she said. “It holds.”

Elara whispered it under her breath, soft as a seed falling: “I will not wear this dress to Blackmoor Hall.”

“What was that, my lady?” The seamstress looked up, a single pin still at her lips.

Elara’s smile held. The mask held. “I said, you are a marvel, Mistress Peveril. Pin it well.”

Margaret was already talking—accounts, guests, the hundred small duties that would carry them to the carriage—and her voice wound around them both, bright and meaningless as candlelight in an empty room. Elara let it roll over her. She stood very still in the white dress, a girl made of silk and patience and painted-on smiles, and behind the mask a spark smoldered.

The carriage would come. The dress would be waiting.

But the dress would be waiting empty. She was still walking; she would be walking still, when the moors turned to sea and the harbor names became a place of stone and salt and no master at all. She said it once more, in the well of her own silence, where only she could hear.

*I will not wear this dress.*

The spark held. The moors went on. She smiled at her reflection, and the reflection smiled back. The mask was flawless. The mask was a door.

And she already knew how the latch worked from the inside.

chapters.name: The Night Before
chapters.content:
The night before the wedding, Thornwood lay still as a held breath.

Elara lay in her bed and watched the darkness take the shape of the room. The canopy above her was a pool of shadow; the window was a faint gray square slowly resolving as her eyes adjusted. She had not slept. She had not tried. For ten nights she had counted them down like a prisoner scratching tally marks, and now the last one was here, and her body felt strange to her—too light, too hollow, as if she had already left it behind.

Somewhere below, the house ticked and settled. A board groaned in the corridor. The wind moved through the eaves like something breathing. She listened to it all with a clarity that felt like fever, cataloging each sound, separating the ordinary from the dangerous.

She had chosen this night for the moon. There was no moon. The sky beyond her window was a black cloth without a single star showing through, and the moors would be a sea of darkness around her. That was what she wanted. That was what she needed.

At the ninth hour, she heard the servants’ footsteps fade down the back stair. Cook’s voice, muffled through the floor, called something to Jem about the morning. The clatter of pots ceased. One by one, the lights in the lower windows guttered out. She counted the silences.

At the tenth hour, Elara rose.

She did not light a candle. She had rehearsed this in her mind so many times that her hands knew the way. Barefoot, in her thin shift, she crossed the cold boards to the armoire and knelt. The bottom drawer slid open without a sound. Her fingers found the folded wool—the mended riding habit, restored by Bess to look as though it had never been torn. The cloth was rough and smelled faintly of cedar. She held it to her face for a moment, not out of sentiment but to know it, to make it part of her body before she put it on.

She dressed in the dark. Riding habit first, over a plain cotton underdress Bess had left folded beneath it. The wool was warm and heavy, a little loose across her shoulders, and she remembered the hollow days with a distant surprise, as if they had happened to someone else. Then her riding boots, soft and worn, laced to the knee. She had worn them the day Storm threw her. The memory came and went without pain.

Her hair she bound tight at the nape of her neck with a strip of leather. No jewelry. No pins. Nothing that could catch the moonlight and betray her.

The grass bracelet was in the pocket of her dressing gown, where she had hidden it during the fitting. She took it out and turned it in her fingers. It was brittle now. The grass had dried and the strand of hair had loosened. She thought of his words in the hunting lodge, spoken in that quiet voice that had first made her see him whole.

*Everything a man makes with his hands breaks. That doesn’t mean he shouldn’t make it.*

She slipped the bracelet over her wrist with great care. The dried grass scraped her skin like a whisper. She would not take it off again. She would bury it with her or she would wear it until it crumbled, and either way it would have been worth the making.

She crossed to the armoire’s right panel and put her hand against the carved rose that hid the catch. She had known it was there since the day after the flogging, when she had run her hands over every surface of the room looking for a way out, and found the grain of the wood shifted beneath her fingers. The panel gave with a soft click. She pushed, and the dark of the passage opened before her like a mouth.

She did not look back at the room. She did not look at the window where she had stood barefoot and counted every blow of the lash. She stepped into the passage and pulled the panel closed behind her.

The servant’s stair was narrower than she remembered, and the darkness was absolute. She laid her palm against the wall—smooth plaster gone cool with disuse—and began to descend. Twenty-three treads. She knew each one. The ninth, the sixteenth, the twentieth complained beneath the foot, so she kept to the edges where the boards had worn hard and silent. She counted them in her head, a litany against the black: *one, two, three*—on the ninth she stepped close to the wall, and the tread held. *Ten, eleven, twelve*—her breath was even. *Sixteen*—she leaned into the stone, and the wood beneath her foot gave a faint, groaning sigh that died without echo.

Twenty-three. She reached the bottom and stood still, listening.

The stillroom door was before her, a rectangle of deeper black in the black. She had never opened it. She had measured it with her eyes from the kitchen passage, had seen the side that faced the servants’ corridor, but she had not dared to test it until tonight, because if it was locked, or if it squealed on its hinges, she needed to know now, with no time left to find another way.

She put her hand on the iron latch. Cold, pitted with rust. She lifted it slowly—the mechanism moved with a dull *clack* that seemed enormous in the silence. She held her breath.

No sound from beyond. No footsteps. No cry.

She pulled the door toward her. The hinges held. They did not cry out. She slipped through into the stillroom, where the air was thick with dried herbs and the ghost of last winter’s fires. Moonless dark pressed in through the high windows, but she did not need light. She knew the path: between the worktable and the shelf of jars, around the old press, to the kitchen passage door.

She paused at the threshold. The kitchen passage led past the buttery, the pantry, the servants’ hall, and then to the latched side door that opened into the herb garden. Bess would be watching the corridor. Bess would have left the bundle under the rosemary bush at the gap in the garden wall. Bess had promised to be the wall between Elara and Martha’s eyes until the moon set.

There was no moon. The moon had set hours ago, or had never risen.

Elara stepped into the passage.

The house breathed around her. She could hear, faintly, the snore of one of the maids through the wall, the scrabble of a mouse in the pantry. She passed the buttery door and the smell of bread and old apples. Her heart was beating very hard now, a drum that seemed to shake her ribs, and she pressed her hand against her chest as if to quiet it.

She reached the corner where the passage turned toward the side door. A few more steps. The door was a faint gray shape in the dark, taller than she remembered, iron-banded, with a latch she had never touched.

Then she heard it.

A footstep. Soft, deliberate, on the stone behind her.

Elara stopped. Her hand found the cold wall. She did not turn.

The footstep came again. Closer. And then a voice, low and quiet, pitched to carry no further than her own ears:

“Going somewhere, my lady?”

Martha.

Elara stood frozen, her back to the voice, her blood a sudden cold sheet over her skin. She heard the maid take another step, and another, and then Martha was beside her in the dark, a shape barely visible, her cap a pale smudge above a face that held nothing at all.

“I thought you might try tonight,” Martha said. “The night before. I thought to myself, she’ll go the night before, when the house is tired and no one is watching. And here you are.”

Elara’s mouth was dry. She forced herself to turn, to face the other woman, to keep her voice level. “Are you going to scream for my father?”

Martha tilted her head. The gesture was almost gentle. “I haven’t decided yet.”

“What do you want?”

“Want?” Martha let out a soft breath that might have been a laugh. “It was never about what I wanted. You think I wanted to spend twenty-two years carrying trays and emptying slops and watching girls like you look through me as if I were glass? You think I wanted to watch him—that man—with his quiet hands and his quiet voice, and know he would never look at me the way he looked at you?”

Elara said nothing.

“I loved him,” Martha said. The words were flat, unadorned, and somehow more terrible for it. “I would have given him everything I had. I offered him my savings. My room. My life. I told him I would go with him, anywhere, and he refused me. *Already spoken for,* he said. And I knew. I knew it was you.”

“Martha.” Elara’s voice came out strange, not quite steady. “You put that chalice in his loft. You had him flogged. You had him thrown out onto the moors with his back in ribbons. If you ever loved him, how can you stand here and speak of it?”

“Because I love him still,” Martha said. “And what is love in this house but the thing that gets destroyed? You would have destroyed him too. You would have run away with him and made him a fugitive, made him die on some dirt road with your father’s riders at his heels. I saved him from that.”

“You delivered him to the lash.”

“I delivered him to the world,” Martha said, “with a chance to live. You would have delivered him to the gallows. So yes, I watched. I watched you go to him in that ruin of a lodge, night after night, and I wrote it all down in my heart so that I could tell your father, and I did, and I would do it again.”

The cold in Elara’s chest was not rage. It was something older and quieter, a kind of recognition. Martha was not mad. Martha was right, in the only way that mattered to her. She had made her choice, and she had made it out of love, and she would burn the world down with it.

“So what now?” Elara said. “You’ll drag me back to my room. You’ll wake my father. He’ll lock me in until the carriage comes, and I’ll marry Lord Vexford, and you’ll have won.”

Martha looked at her for a long moment. In the dark, her face was unreadable.

“But then,” she said slowly, “he’ll still be out there. And you’ll still be here. And I’ll still be watching.”

Elara waited.

Martha reached up and smoothed her apron, a small, prim gesture. “Go,” she said.

Elara did not move. “What?”

“Go,” Martha repeated. “I didn’t stop you. I never stopped you.” She stepped aside, leaving the passage clear. “I wanted you to know that I saw you. That I knew. That you didn’t slip out of this house like a ghost through a wall—that a living woman watched you go, and chose not to call out. That is the only gift I will ever give you, and I give it to him, not to you. I give it to him because I love him, and because I know he is out there, and because I know that if you find him, you will tell him that Martha let you go.”

Her voice broke on the last word. It was the first genuine sound Elara had ever heard from her.

Elara opened her mouth. She did not know what she meant to say. Something rose in her throat—gratitude, or horror, or a strange, unwilling pity—but Martha shook her head.

“Don’t,” Martha said. “Don’t thank me. Don’t speak to me again. Go now, before I remember that I love him, and that you are the reason he will never love me back.”

Elara moved. She did not run, because running would make noise. She walked past Martha, close enough to smell the lye soap on her hands and the wool of her apron, and then she reached the side door.

Her hand closed on the latch. It was cold, and the iron was rough, and for a moment she thought it would not lift.

It lifted.

The door swung inward on silent hinges—Bess had oiled them. The night air rushed in, cold and wet and vast, smelling of earth and grass and the open moor.

Elara stepped through into the herb garden. The door closed behind her with a soft click, and she stood in the blackness, trembling, the breath tearing past her teeth.

A shape moved in the dark beside the rosemary bush. For a moment her heart seized—but it was small, and it rose, and Bess’s voice came to her, barely a whisper:

“Go. The bundle is at the gap. Storm is bridled and waiting. I told Jem there was a stone in his hoof and he needed walking.” A pause. “I oiled the side gate too.”

Elara reached out and found Bess’s hand in the dark. She squeezed it. Bess squeezed back, once, hard, and then let go.

Elara did not look back. She crossed the garden with her arms wrapped around herself, feeling the wind come off the moors like a living thing, and at the gap in the wall by the apple trees she found the bundle—a wool cloak, a loaf, a heel of cheese, a flint and steel, a blade wrapped in oilcloth. She shrugged the cloak over her shoulders. It was too big, and it smelled of the kitchen, and it was warm.

She passed through the gap.

The moors opened before her, an emptiness without horizon. No moon. No stars. Just the wind and the black and the distant shape of the stables, a lower blackness against the sky.

Inside, the horses shifted in their stalls. Storm’s head came up as she entered, ears pricked, and she spoke his name in a low voice that surprised her with its steadiness. He was already saddled—Bess had done that too, or Jem, or someone who had chosen to look away. The leather was warm where the blanket had lain, and the horse shivered, not with fear but with readiness.

Elara led him out of the stable. He moved beside her with that big, eager stride she had always loved, the stride that carried her over the moors like a ship over the sea. She set her foot in the stirrup and swung up. The saddle creaked. The wind lifted her hair.

She turned Storm’s head east.

The drove road was a pale scar through the heather, barely visible in the dark. She did not need to see it. She had walked it in her mind a thousand times. She had memorized the old map in Pryce’s ledger: the drove road to Coldwell, the track that branched at the leaning stone, the ford marked with a cross where the stream bent double. Beyond that, she had only a rumor. A scarred man living rough in a fishing village on the eastern coast. A man who came out of the moors and would speak of nothing but the sea.

She touched the grass bracelet on her wrist.

“I am still walking,” she whispered into the wind.

Storm surged forward. The gate was open—Bess had opened it, or left it unlatched, or the wind had taken it—and they passed through it together, out of the garden, out of the yard, out of the reach of Thornwood’s walls.

Behind her, the house stood dark and silent. She did not look back. She did not see the pale shape at the east window—her mother, perhaps, or Martha, or no one at all. She only rode east, into the moonless dark, following a rumor of a man she loved.

chapters.name: The Peddler's Rumor
chapters.content:
The night had no stars. Elara rode east with the dark pressed against her like a wall she had to keep pushing through, Storm moving beneath her with a long, reaching stride. The grass bracelet was a dry whisper against her wrist. She had not taken it off since she had slipped it on in the darkness of Thornwood, and she did not intend to.

The drove road unrolled ahead, a paler ribbon of packed earth between the black slopes of heather. She knew the map by heart—the one she had traced in lamplight in what felt like another life, her finger following the ink line east from Thornwood's red boundary. The road would carry her to Coldwell if she stayed on it, but she did not want the port. She wanted the rumor. A scarred man. A fishing village. A man who came out of the moors and spoke of nothing but the sea.

She recited the harbor names under her breath as she rode, the way he had taught her in the hunting lodge: Coldwell, Blackwater, Saltcombe, Rook's Reach. They had been his prayer once. Now they were hers. She said them in rhythm with Storm's hooves, a litany against the dark and against the terrible possibility that she was riding east toward a man who no longer existed.

The moon did not rise. The stars stayed hidden. She rode blind, trusting the horse and the pale road and the map inside her skull, and she did not weep. She had done enough weeping in the weeks of staring at the moors. Now there was only the hard, physical act of escape, which was less like flying and more like running with something heavy in her arms.

Storm's stride faltered as the night wore on. She felt it in his shoulders, a loss of rhythm. She pulled him down to a walk before he could ask, and when the sky began to gray along the eastern edge like a coal breathing its first heat, she found what she was looking for: a stand of hawthorns huddled in a fold of the land, the stream from the map bending around them.

The ford.

She reined in at the water's edge. The stream was shallow and clear, running over stones the color of pewter. Storm lowered his head and drank. She dismounted stiffly, almost falling, her ankle protesting. She had been ignoring the ache for weeks. It would not break now.

She led Storm to the deepest part of the stream. While he drank, she looked out at the gray world beginning to wake. The fog had thinned. The horizon had a shape. She could see the low place where the drove road skirted a bog, and the broken tooth of a standing stone leaning against the sky.

The old shepherd's wall was somewhere near. The cache. Bread, cheese, a waterskin, a blanket. He had hidden it months ago, when the plan had been different, when they had thought they would have more time. He had walked east, beaten and barefoot, with nothing but his life. If he had reached the wall, he would have found the cache. If he had lain down in the heather before that, he would have died.

She did not know.

She said his name out loud, alone in the gray morning, and the sound of it startled her. "Kael," she said, and then, quieter, "I am still walking."

Storm stamped and shook water from his muzzle. She pulled the bundle from behind the saddle and ate a heel of the bread and a piece of the hard cheese, standing with her shoulder against the horse's warm flank. The cheese was bitter. The bread was stale. She ate it slowly because she had learned in the hollow days that food eaten too fast made her ill.

She let Storm graze for an hour. She sat on a stone and unlaced her boot, checking her ankle. It was swollen but not badly, and the swelling was old and familiar. She thought about her father. The breakfast tray would arrive at her room and find it empty. The chambermaid would call out. Then the house would wake in earnest, and her father would stand in the middle of her stripped room with his iron face, reaching for the men he would send east.

She had a start of maybe a day. It was not enough. She tightened her boot, mounted Storm, and turned east.

The land changed slowly. The heather thinned, the ground grew sandier, the sky broader. She caught the smell of the sea long before she could see it, a cold mineral sharpness riding the wind at her back. She had never seen the sea. She had read about it in the cracked-spine book in the library, with his shoulder nearly touching hers. No wall, no gate, no master.

By mid-afternoon Storm was limping.

She felt it before she saw it. She dismounted and ran a hand down his near foreleg, finding a stone wedged in the hoof. She had watched the grooms at Thornwood do this a hundred times. She had never done it herself. She knelt in the dust of the road, took his hoof in her hands, and worked the stone free, speaking to him in a low, steady voice.

"There. It's out."

Storm nosed her shoulder. She laughed, a rusty sound that surprised her. Then she was nearly weeping, and she forced the tears back down into the well where she kept the harbor names.

The sun was low, throwing long shadows, when she came to the crossroads.

It was a lonely place. A single gnarled thorn tree stood where the roads met, bent by years of wind until it pointed east. A water trough, dry. No house, no inn, no shelter.

And the peddler.

She saw him when he was still far off. A cart with a canvas tilt sagging over its load, drawn by a patient brown mule. The man walking beside it was small and wiry, wrapped in a coat patched so many times it was more patch than coat, and he carried a long staff in one hand and a clay pipe in the other.

He saw her at the same moment. He did not slow his mule. He took the pipe out of his mouth, spat into the dust, and called in a voice as dry as the road: "Fair morning to you, or fair evening, whichever the wind hasn't taken. You lost?"

"No," she said. "Riding east."

"East is a long road." He came abreast of her, and she saw his eyes move over her face, her boots, the grass bracelet on her wrist. He was not a man who missed much. "A long road and a lonely one, for a young woman with no servant and no escort."

"I prefer it."

"Aye." He nodded, as if that were the most reasonable answer in the world. "I've known a few who prefer the lonely roads. Most are running from something. Some are running to something. Some don't know the difference, and that's the worst kind, because they'll run until they run off the edge of the earth." He leaned on his staff. "Which are you?"

"I'm looking for someone."

"Aye. Everyone's looking for someone. Who's the someone?"

She hesitated. She had not said it to anyone, had had no one to say it to. The rumor had come to her through a whispered memory, a servant's gossip carried to Bess's ears by a drover's cousin. A scarred man. A fishing village. She lifted her chin.

"A tall man," she said. "Scarred on his back. He came out of the moors some weeks ago, barefoot, with nothing. He might have been looking for work in the villages on the coast."

The peddler was quiet for a long moment. He drew on his pipe, let the smoke drift, and watched her with eyes that had seen too many stories to be surprised by another.

"Coast's a long stretch," he said. "Lots of villages. Lots of men with scars. You'll need to be more particular."

"Have you heard of such a man?"

"I hear a lot of things on the roads. People talk to a peddler the way they talk to a priest, because they don't think he'll repeat it." He smiled, showing a gap in his teeth. "They're wrong about that. I'll trade anything, including information, for the right price."

She had nothing to trade. She had known it before she spoke. The bundle behind her saddle held only bread and cheese and flint and steel and a blade. No coin. No silver. Her father had kept her penniless the way he had kept her locked in her room.

She looked at her hands, raw from the reins, and then at the bracelet on her wrist. She would not trade that.

But there was the ring. Her mother had given it to her on her sixteenth birthday with a strange, distracted look, as if seeing someone else in Elara's face. A thin gold band set with pale stone the color of sea glass. She had worn it because it was easier than explaining why she didn't want it.

She pulled it off and held it out.

"I have this. Gold, and the stone is real."

The peddler looked at the ring in her open palm. He reached out and took it, turning it in his calloused fingers.

"Sea glass," he said. "Not worth much. But it's honest, and there's enough here to cover a story or two." He tucked it into his coat. "I'll tell you what I know, and I'll tell you true."

She nodded.

"I was through the eastern villages three weeks back," he said. "Working the coast road from Saltcombe up to Blackwater, selling mended pots and buttons and thread nobody needs but everybody buys. The place I remember is a little village, no name worth saying—a scatter of cottages around a harbor that dries out at low tide. Gulls. Nets. The kind of place where a stranger stands out." He paused and scratched his chin. "There was a man there. Came in about two weeks back, maybe less. Walking. On his own. He looked like he'd been dragged behind a horse."

Elara's hands tightened on the reins.

"The woman who took him in, widow named Gorse, hard woman with a hard tongue but she took him in anyway. Said he'd walked out of the moors and collapsed in her yard with his back in ribbons. She thought he was a deserter or a thief. He told her he was none of those."

"What did he tell her?"

"Nothing much. That's the thing. The man barely spoke. But what he did say was about the sea. She said he'd sit on the harbor wall at dusk and say the names of places under his breath like he was praying. Coldwell, Blackwater, Saltcombe, Rook's Reach. She heard him at it once. Called him touched, but harmless. He did odd work. Mended a net. Wouldn't take coin, just food and a corner of her shed."

The peddler looked at Elara squarely.

"He's scarred, that one. Back and chest both, and the chest scar's older. But it's his back that would turn your stomach. She said he never takes his shirt off where anyone can see, but she saw it the first night when she was cleaning the wounds, and she said if she ever met the man who did that to him, she'd take a skillet to his head. She's not a woman who makes threats idle."

Elara's throat was so tight she could barely speak. "He's still there? The village—is he still there?"

"I don't know. I left the coast three days ago. He was there when I left, sitting on the harbor wall, talking to the sea." The peddler looked at her for a long moment, and his voice softened. "If it's the same man—and I think it is, because I don't believe there are two men walking out of the moors with their backs cut to bone saying the names of northern harbors like a prayer—then you'll find him. Take the coast road south from Saltcombe. It's half a day's ride past Blackwater. The village you want has a red door on the chapel and a broken jetty like a finger pointing at the sea."

He shifted his weight.

"What's his name?" he asked. "So I know the story's worth the telling."

She almost said it. The syllable was on her lips, kept hot like a coal. But she had not survived her father's house to become a fool on an empty road.

"He'll know me," she said.

The peddler studied her. Then he nodded slowly.

"Aye, I expect he will." He touched a finger to his forehead in a gesture that was almost a salute. "Ride on, then. Light's going. There's a shepherd's hut about two miles east along this road, dry enough if you don't mind the mice. You'll reach the coast by morning."

"Thank you," she said.

"Don't thank me." He was already turning his mule toward the northern road. "I only told you what you paid for. Whether the man's still there when you arrive—that's between you and the sea."

He raised a hand once, and then he was gone, a dark shape moving away through the long shadows, trailing a thin thread of pipe smoke.

She sat at the crossroads for a long moment. The sun was nearly down. The wind had turned cold, sharp with the smell of the coast she could not yet see. She looked at the pale band of unweathered skin where the ring had been.

She did not regret it.

He was alive. He had come out of the moors. He had collapsed in a widow's yard with his back in ribbons, and he had risen, and he had gone to the harbor wall and said the harbor names like a prayer. He had been waiting.

She touched the grass bracelet. The dried grass was brittle, the dark strand of hair among the fibers loosened with the riding. She pressed it flat against her wrist, holding it there.

Coldwell. Blackwater. Saltcombe. Rook's Reach.

She said the names in order, in his voice and then in hers, and the sound of them in the empty crossroads settled something in her chest.

"A red door," she said to Storm, and the horse's ear flicked back. "A broken jetty. A man on the harbor wall."

It was not a plan. It was better than a plan. It was the shape of him, drawn in rumor and salt, and she would follow it until the shape had flesh again.

She touched her heels to Storm's sides, and the horse moved forward willingly, as if he could smell the sea too. The road ran on through the deepening dusk, and as she rode she let herself imagine the harbor, the nets, the stones of the wall under his hands. She imagined his head turning, the slow recognition in his face, the sound of her name from a throat that had been silent for weeks.

She kept her hand on the bracelet and rode on into the night, and for the first time in weeks, hope was not a weight in her chest. It was a second heart, beating alongside the first, keeping time with the rhythm of the horse's stride and the names she whispered into the wind.

chapters.name: The Village by the Sea
chapters.content:
**Chapter 25: The Village by the Sea**

The second day was all fog and rain. It came off the sea before she reached the sea, a gray damp that found its way in at the throat of the kitchen cloak and down the laced tops of her boots and along the strip of leather binding her hair, until the cold was in everything she owned and she was hollowed out, filled with weather. Elara rode with her hood up and her head down, reciting the harbor names in rhythm with Storm's hooves—Coldwell, Blackwater, Saltcombe, Rook's Reach—until the words lost their edges and became a pulse, a charm, a litany to hold the dark at bay.

The land changed as she went. The heather thinned to wiry grass, then to sand and ditches of brackish water the fog turned to pewter. She passed no one. Twice she heard hoofbeats somewhere behind and pulled Storm into the lee of whatever cover the road offered, her hand on his muzzle, feeling the tremor that ran through him—his answer to a call she would not let him make. Both times the sound dwindled and died.

Near midday she stopped at a shepherd's hut the peddler had marked in her memory. She gave Storm the last of the oats and sat on the packed-earth floor with her knees drawn up, eating the heel of the loaf until it was gone. Her ankle ached with its old, familiar insistence. Pain was company, at least. It meant she was still inside her body, and her body was still moving east.

The fog thinned in midafternoon, not all at once but in tatters, and through a tatter she saw the sea.

Elara had never seen the sea. She had read about it in a book with a cracked spine, sitting close to a man who could not read, teaching him the words for water and wind and distance. "No wall, no gate, no master." She had thought she understood. But the book had not told her how gray it was, how the gray of the water met the gray of the sky until the world softened at the edges and there was no horizon, only a place where everything exhaled. The sea breathed. It climbed the sand in long, unhurried strokes and fell back with a sound like a held breath released.

Storm stopped of his own accord, ears forward, nostrils flared. She let him stand.

"Coldwell," she said aloud. "Blackwater. Saltcombe. Rook's Reach." The names were different here. They tasted like the truth.

The coast road ran south along the edge of the land. The village appeared in the falling light as a huddle of cottages around a harbor standing empty at low tide, the boats leaning in the mud like old men sleeping. A chapel stood at the far end of the lane, its door painted red—bright in the wet air as a wound—and a broken jetty pointed at the sea like a finger.

A man in a tarred coat was coiling rope on the quay. He looked up at the sound of her horse, took her in—a lady on a gray gelding in a maid's cloak, soaked through—and his face opened a little.

"Widow Gorse's man," he said. She had not asked. "Net-shed at the end of the row. He'll be there."

"He sits on the wall at dusk, saying his words."

The man shrugged. "Gorse says he's touched. I say he's praying for someone. Either way, he's there."

The net-shed leaned against the wind as if it had long ago let the weather have its way, tarred planks gray with salt, one small window shuttered. A line of lamplight fell through the gap under the door and lay across the wet stones. Elara dismounted and tied Storm to an iron ring in the wall, her hands cramped from the reins, and stood at the door. Beneath the sound of the sea she heard a small movement within.

She lifted the latch. It lifted.

The door swung open, and the lamplight spilled out, and she saw him.

He sat among coils of netting with his back to the door, a mended shirt hanging open at the shoulders. The shirt was thin, and what it covered was scored into his skin: twenty lashes healed into a lattice of raised scars, silvered across his shoulders and ribs, crossing and recrossing the back she knew as intimately as she knew the harbor names. He held a piece of bread in one hand. He had not turned at the hoofbeats, or had not believed them, or did not dare.

She said his name.

The bread fell. It struck the packed-earth floor and rolled, and the sound was very loud in the small room. He turned slowly, like a man who has practiced bearing bad news alone, and the lamplight found his face.

Elara felt the ground shift. He was thinner than she had ever seen him, the bones of his face standing out as if pushed up from inside. A rough beard shaded his jaw, making him look older, harder, carved from the coast. The old scar crossed his chest where the shirt fell open, older than Thornwood, older than either of them. He was gaunt and hollow and shabby, with crumbs in his beard, and his eyes were the same.

Those eyes. That was what broke her.

For a moment neither spoke. The sea breathed behind the hut. A gull cried once and was not answered.

Elara stood in the doorway with the rain dripping from her hood and the grass bracelet cold against her wrist, and every word she had rehearsed on the long road east deserted her. They lay scattered behind her on the moors. She could not remember one.

Kael rose. He set the bread down on the netting with absurd, careful precision, and crossed the room in three strides. She thought he would take her in his arms. She wanted him to. But he stopped a hand's breadth away, close enough that she felt the heat of him through the damp wool, and reached out and took her hand. Her right hand, the one with the bracelet beneath the sleeve. When his hand closed around hers, something in her chest unclenched that she had not known she was holding. It was not relief. It was not joy. It was home.

He turned her wrist over and drew the soaked cuff back. The grass bracelet lay against her skin, dark with wet, worn thin, the strand of his hair loosened from the braid and afloat against the pale inside of her arm. He looked at it a long time.

"You kept it," he said. His voice was rough, as if he had not used it in days.

"I never took it off. Not once. Not in the house, not on the road. I told myself I'd bury it with me if I had to."

His thumb moved over the dried grass, careful not to break it. When he raised his eyes to hers they were bright, but he did not weep. "You're soaked," he said.

"I've been riding for two days. I've been saying your name into the fog. The peddler said you were here, and I didn't believe him, and then I saw the red door, and I still didn't believe it, because I kept thinking you were dead." Her voice cracked, and she pulled it down into the well where she kept the harbor names, and let it rest. "You're alive."

"I am," he said gently. "You're the reason I am."

"How do you know that?"

He looked at her, and she saw the tally of the long days behind his eyes: the harbor wall at dusk, the cold, the sea saying nothing back. "I sat on the wall every evening and said the names until I ran out, and then I started again. I was saying them for you, so that if you ever said them back, I would know where I was."

"I said them," Elara said. "All the way east. I said them until I heard the sea answer."

His hand tightened around hers. "I found the cache," he said. "At the shepherd's wall. The bread, the cheese, the waterskin. I'd hidden it for us—for the night we meant to run—and then I ate it alone, sitting in the heather, telling myself you hadn't sent me any farther than I could go." He paused. "I thought about lying down there and not getting up. But the blanket was in the cache. You'd have wanted it for the road. I wrapped it around my shoulders and I walked."

He drew her inside and pulled the door shut. The latch clicked, and for a moment the wet and the fog and the rest of the world were sealed out, and there was only the small room: a brazier burning low, a pallet of straw and sacks, coils of mended nets, a tin cup, a folded shirt, a stub of candle guttering. The room of a man who owned nothing and wanted less. There were wounds here, too, older than his back, and she saw them and loved him for them.

She reached for the open collar of his shirt, to the edge of the old scar on his chest, the one from before Thornwood, the one she had never asked about. She did not touch it. She hovered, afraid.

"Does it still hurt?" she asked. "Your back."

"The skin healed." He said it without drama. "It healed wrong. It pulls, and it will pull for the rest of my life. But it healed." He was watching her face. "What hurt was looking up at that east window and not being able to go back through the gate."

"I watched them tie you to the post. I watched you take every blow and not make a sound."

"I knew you were listening."

"I counted them all. I counted them on my own skin. I couldn't feel anything else for days."

He took her face in his hands, callused and gentle. "You don't have to count them anymore. I'm here. You're here. Whatever comes next, you're not alone in it." Only "not alone" was too small a word for what he was offering her; she heard the rest of it anyway, in the set of his jaw and the way his thumb moved once along her cheekbone.

"No wall," she said. "No gate. No master."

The ghost of a smile crossed his face, gone like light on water. "And a door," he said. "And a table. And a garden." The promises from the hunting lodge, from the library, from the dark. "I never got to make any of them."

"We'll make them together," she said.

A hard rapping came at the door, and the latch lifted before either of them could move. A woman pushed in—square and weathered as the coast itself, gray hair scraped back, a clay pot in her hands. She stopped at the sight of Elara and looked her over without hurry: the soaked cloak, the riding habit beneath it, the lady's hands.

"So you're the one," she said. "He's been talking to the sea about you for two weeks. I thought he was touched. I still think he's touched." She thrust the pot at Elara. "Stew. It's thin, but it's hot. Eat it, and then stop dripping on my floor." To Kael she said, "You'll be gone before dawn, I suppose."

"Yes," Kael said.

"Good. I'll keep the horse fed and the door shut. Whatever you're running from, I don't want to know its name, and I'd thank you not to say it under my roof." She looked at Elara again, and her eyes were older than her face. "He said you'd come. I told him he was a fool. I've known too many men who waited on the sea for a woman who never came." She pulled the door open, letting in the sound of the water. "He's a good man. Be worth the waiting."

She was gone before Elara could answer.

Kael took the pot from Elara's hands and set it by the brazier. He reached for her face, and this time she leaned into it, and he kissed her forehead, her temple, the wet hair at her parting—slowly, as if he had all the time in the world and meant to spend it here. It was the first time in weeks that anyone had touched her without wanting something in return.

"We need to be gone before dawn," he said against her hair. "He'll have found the room empty by now. He'll send riders east—he knows I walked east, and he knows you'll come looking for me. By tomorrow night they'll be on the coast."

"Then we go before dawn. I didn't come all this way to be taken back."

He nodded, and then his eyes went past her to the door. "Storm. He carried you all the way here."

"He did. A stone came up in his hoof south of the ford. I took it out myself." She saw his face change. "Don't look at me like that. You weren't there to do it."

"Like what?"

"Like you're proud of me."

The ghost of a smile came and went. "I've been proud of you since the day you brought me a book and taught me to read it. The stone is only the latest thing." He let her go, gently. "I'll see to him before first light—grain him, run a hand over his shoes. He'll need to be strong for the road."

He drew back to look at her. His eyes moved over her face, reading the changes: the hollows, the set of her mouth, the hard new thing that lived behind her eyes. He did not flinch from it. "Your mother's ring," he said. "You wore it."

She lifted her hand, and he saw the pale band of unweathered skin where the ring had been. "I traded it to a peddler for the way here. It bought me you."

It was not possible for a smile to be both so glad and so grave, but his was. "I'll buy you another," he said. "I don't know how. I don't know when. But I will."

She believed him. She had believed him when he had braided dried grass and a strand of his own hair into a bracelet and told her a man makes things that break and makes them anyway, and she believed him now, in a borrowed shirt in a net-shed at the edge of the sea, with the marks of the lash crossing his back and the old scar over his heart.

Outside, the fog lay thick on the water. The village slept. The sea went on breathing against the shore, keeping time. Elara stood in the circle of the brazier's light with the man she loved, and she did not think about the riders, or the carriage, or the white dress waiting empty in a locked room far away. She thought only of the cottage by the sea, the door he would build, the table he would set, the shelf for the sea book, the garden where heather grew.

*I am still walking.*

And for one night, in a village by the sea, she was home.

chapters.name: Two Days Behind
chapters.content:
The sea woke her first—a change of sound, a slackening of the tide against the jetty stones. Then Kael's hand was on her shoulder, a light pressure that had learned gentleness in a hard life, and she came up out of sleep with her heart already running.

"Not yet light," he said. "We go now."

The village had not woken. A single lamp burned in Widow Gorse's window—she had made them wait while she pulled the bread from her morning bake, cursed the hour, and refused every word of thanks with a turn of her back. The loaf steamed inside its sacking. The cheese was hard as a stone and smelled of the goat-shed, and Elara held both against her chest as if they were the last food in the world.

Kael led Storm out from behind the net-shed, saddled and grain-fed, his coat already dark with the fog that rolled off the water. He worked quickly, in a silence that said he had been awake long before her, checking every strap, reading the dark for weather, putting miles between themselves and the village before the fishermen came down to the boats.

She mounted first, and he swung up behind her. The horse grunted, stepped sideways, then settled. Kael's arms came around her to take the reins, and for a moment she felt the whole length of him against her back—the thinness of him, the new hardness of the scars that pulled at his shoulders beneath the mended shirt—and she thought, *This is what it is to be carried*.

They rode north along the coast road at a walk, sparing the horse, keeping to the grass verge where the ground was soft enough to muffle their passage. The village fell away behind them—the red chapel door, the broken jetty like a finger pointing at the sea—until the fog took it and left only the sound of the water and the crying of gulls waking over the shallows.

They did not speak for the first mile. The only sounds were the creak of saddle leather, the horse's breathing, the soft slide of hooves through wet sand. The sea was on their left, gray meeting gray without a horizon, the same seamlessness she had seen from the shepherd's hut two days before, and she understood now why Kael had sat on the harbor wall talking to it. The sea did not ask what you had done. The sea did not keep ledgers.

"The riders," she said at last, "will have reached the coast by tonight."

"Aye." He said it without alarm, the way a man states a fact about weather. "They'll come at it from the west, the way you came. They'll ask at every village between the ford and the shore. They'll hear about the woman who rode east on a gray horse, and they'll expect her to be trying for a port with a ship in it."

"Coldwell. Saltcombe. Rook's Reach."

"They'll watch all of them," he agreed. "So we don't go to the sea. We leave it here."

She turned her head, and the movement brought her cheek close to his jaw. He smelled of smoke and salt and the cheap soap Gorse had left by the well. "Where do we go?"

"North." He nodded at the land rising on their right: the green edge of the coast giving way to a darker line of heather and broken stone. "There's a drove road cuts inland past an old shepherd's wall, about four miles north. I found it the day after the flogging. I walked along it half a morning before the pain turned me around. It crosses empty country—no villages, no wayposts, nothing but moor and sky until you're past the rivers. Men on horseback can follow a coast road. They can't follow you through the heather."

"You walked that far? With your back—"

"Not far enough." He said it without self-pity, a simple correction. "I turned back. Sat down in the heather and thought about not getting up. But I remembered the way."

The road curved inland as the sun rose, a pale wash behind the cloud, and they left the sound of the sea behind them. For a while Elara kept looking back over her shoulder, expecting to see the ruined jetty again, but the land had folded itself shut as if the village had never been. Only the smell of salt and the gulls' cries followed them a little way, growing fainter, until the wind changed and carried only the smell of wet peat and heather.

They stopped at mid-morning under a low ridge where a spring seeped out of the ground and cut a muddy wound through the grass. Storm drank. They drank, cupping the cold water in their hands, tasting iron and peat and the cold of the earth. Kael tore the bread in two and gave her the larger piece. She broke the smaller piece and gave it back, and they stood looking at each other with bread in both hands, and the absurdity of it nearly made her laugh.

"We'll be hungry again by dark," he said. "Eat it."

"So will you."

"I've been hungrier. Eat."

She ate. The bread was coarse and warm and tasted like the kitchen at Gorse's that she had never entered, and she thought of Bess's small war of bread—the loaves smuggled, the kindnesses hidden where Martha could not see them—and her throat closed so suddenly she could not swallow.

Kael saw it. He said nothing, only reached out and took her wrist—the right one, above the grass bracelet—and held it until she swallowed.

"Bess," she said. "She helped me. She kept the side door unlatched. She saddled Storm. She stood between Martha and my door, Kael. If my father finds out any of it—"

"Your father's going to be busy finding you. That's what you fought for." He let her wrist go slowly, his fingers dragging across the dried grass as if he could not quite bear to release it. "Bess is smart. She knows how to look empty and simple. She'll have cried all the right tears and wrung all the right hands. And you'll write to her. One day. We'll find a way to get her a letter."

He was certain because he had to be. She wanted that certainty badly enough to believe him.

They walked on, leading Storm now to spare him the double weight. The track Kael remembered was little more than a scar across the land, two pale lines of worn earth winding between outcrops of gray stone. The moors opened around them, vast and empty and furred with heather not yet in bloom, and the wind moved across it in waves that made the surface of the land seem to shift and breathe. There was no wall, no gate, no master here. Nothing but the fold of the ground and the long line of the sky.

By afternoon the story came out of her—Martha. She had not meant to tell it yet, but hunger and exhaustion had loosened something in her, and the words came up like water from the spring. The interception at the side door. The confession in the dark passage, the confession spoken as if she were already dead. The message.

"She said to tell you," Elara said, "that Martha let you go."

Kael walked on for several steps before he answered. She watched the set of his scarred shoulders under the thin shirt and could not read him.

"I knew," he said. "The morning they dragged me to the post. I looked across the courtyard and I saw her face—I knew it had been her that told. But she let you go." He stopped, and stood with the wind pulling at the loose ends of his shirt. "She loved me the way you love a thing you know you'll never be allowed to keep. I refused her, and she broke it anyway. Not gently. But she did it."

"You're not angry at her?"

"Aye. I'm angry. I'm also grateful, and I'm sorry for her, and I wish I'd never been born good-looking enough to be loved twice and wise enough to keep neither of them safe." He turned to face her. "Martha'll be all right. She's hard."

"She was crying."

"Then she wanted to be. Martha always got what she paid for, in the end."

He said it without cruelty, and it was the closest thing to forgiveness she thought he could offer. She took the grass bracelet between her fingers and turned it, feeling the dried strands brittle against her skin, and they walked on into the long light of the afternoon.

The drove road turned at the shepherd's wall—a tumbled line of dry stone running crooked across the moor, and Kael stopped there a moment, resting his hand on the stones as a man touches a person remembered. Elara understood. This was the place. The cache he had found, bread and cheese and a blanket left by a woman who had trusted a dream. He stood in silence; then he put his hand down and walked on.

They slept in the lee of an abandoned shepherd's hut that had lost its roof and kept only two walls standing against the wind. Kael made her lie down where the bracken had grown thickest and heaped bracken over her legs while she protested. He tethered Storm in the angle where the walls met, unsaddled him, and rubbed him down with a handful of dried grass while the big horse leaned into the work with his eyes half closed.

"Does your back hurt?" she asked.

"Healing scars pull," he said. "That's all. Pulling's not hurting."

"Kael."

He came to her then, still holding the grass in his hands, and knelt down over her where she lay in the bracken. The light was going, a long gray dusk settling over the moor like the tide.

"Does your back hurt?" she said again, softer.

He looked at her for a long moment. "Every step. You?"

"Every step," she said. It was the truest thing she had ever said. His hand found hers in the bracken, and they lay holding on to each other while the wind went over the ruined walls, and the darkness came.

They woke to the dark, ate the last of the cheese, and walked on through the night. There was a moon behind the cloud, enough to see the pale track and the shapes of stones. They did not risk the drove road any longer—by now, Kael reasoned, Aldous's men could have reached it, could be riding the same line of the wall looking for tracks. They cut south of the road instead, straight across the open moor, trusting the fold of the land to hide them and the deep country to swallow their footprints.

The ground was rough. Heather roots caught at her boots; peat bogs glittered with false solidity under the moon, and twice he pulled her back from ground that would have swallowed her to the knee. They moved in a silence broken only by the tack of Storm's bridle and the steady rhythm of their breathing. She had stopped being tired. She had passed through tiredness into a strange, floating clarity, the state of a candle that burns low and sudden bright before it gutters.

It was in that clarity, near dawn, that they saw the riders.

They came over a distant ridge from the east, a string of dark shapes against the first gray band of the sky, too far to be counted clearly, moving northwest. Not a hunting party. A patrol, spread out, searching the land in a line. Kael pulled her down into a shallow ditch where a dry stream ran, and they lay flat among the reeds with the wool cloak pulled over them both while Storm stood stone-still behind them, turned so his dark coat might read as a rock in the half-light.

The riders passed a mile off, riding steadily, harness jingling faintly on the wind, then gone down the far side of the ridge. Kael let out a breath he had been holding for a long time.

"Who were they?" she whispered.

"Heading for the coast," he said. "Probably. Aldous will have men on every road to the harbors by now." He lay beside her, his face close to hers in the ditch, the reeds throwing shadows across his eyes. "We're not on their map. That's the only thing we've got."

"That was close."

"That was far." He touched her face, once, a quick brush of fingers across her temple, as if he were checking that she was still solid. "By tomorrow they'll be two days behind us, and two days behind has to be enough."

But they walked on, and the land rose and fell around them, and the sun came up gray and cold over an empty world. They had nothing left to eat. They had a skin of water from the last stream and a stone-hard crust of bread Kael had saved without telling her, and he made her eat it while he ate nothing and would not say so. She knew. She broke it in half anyway, and they ate it together, standing in the wind on a bare hill, watching the morning widen around them.

She thought of the cottage by the sea then. A door, a table, a shelf for the sea book. A garden where heather grew, though she knew heather grew wild and needed no garden. She thought of children with his steady hands and her sharp eyes, and she thought, *If we die out here, at least we die still walking together.*

But they did not die. The day passed somehow, in the way all things pass if you keep moving. They found a hollow in the heather where a furze bush had died and left a bare bowl of earth, and they lay down in it together, wrapped in the wool cloak, with Storm grazing placidly at the end of his tether as if he had always been a moor pony and had never known a stable.

Night came. Kael's arms tightened around her. The wind spoke its long words over the heather, and the stars came out cold and close.

"We'll make the rivers by tomorrow," he said. "There'll be villages on the other side. Work. Food."

"And a door," she said. "And a table."

"And a garden." His breath stirred her hair. "I'll buy you another ring. I don't know how. I don't know when. But I will."

"Kael."

"Mmm."

"I am still walking."

Against her back, in the dark, she felt him smile—a small movement, a setting down of a weight. "I am still walking," he said. "We'll be all right. Two days behind is a long way."

She did not know if he believed it. But she held on to the words the way she held on to the harbor names, a prayer repeated into the dark until it became a shape she could carry.

Coldwell. Blackwater. Saltcombe. Rook's Reach.

The sea, somewhere behind them, kept on breathing.

They slept.

chapters.name: The Fever Dream of Flight
chapters.content:
The fog had burned off by noon, but the distance did not know what to do with itself. It lay there, heather and gray stone and the low breathing of the wind, and Elara walked into it until her legs forgot they had ever done anything else.

They found a farmyard in the middle of the day: a hovel of stone and turf, a byre leaning like a man considering sitting down, two hens scratching in the mud. No smoke, no dog. Kael put his hand on her arm.

"Stay here. Storm'll graze. Give me two minutes."

She watched him cross the yard with that careful economy she had come to know, the way a man walks who has learned the ground might not hold him and has decided to walk on it anyway. He disappeared into the byre. The hens regarded her with flat indifference. When he came back he carried a small sack of turnips and a clay jug.

"Byre was open. Nobody's milked since yesterday. Turnips are soft. Jug's rain-catch water."

"Did you—" She couldn't finish the sentence.

"Left a copper in the feed trough. If the widow finds a copper and no jug, she'll think she dropped it. If she finds neither, she'll know she was robbed, and she'll tell the next rider."

She considered this. The turnips were small and wizened. She was too hungry to find them anything but beautiful.

They ate sitting against a low stone wall out of the wind, and he taught her, chewing, to eat the skins, because the dirt had salt in it, and she needed the salt. She ate the grit between her teeth and did not mind. The grit was the flavor of the ground, and the ground was holding her up.

That afternoon he taught her to read the land. Not with names exactly—half his words for the folds and hollows seemed invented, or learned so long ago he had forgotten they were words. The long dip where the wind died was "the pocket." The bank of white stone that kept rain off better than a roof was "the shelf." The narrow V where two slopes met, where water would run in a storm and where a rider would look last because it was so obvious, was "the seam."

He stopped once and pointed at a fold of ground she would have crossed without seeing. "You see the darker grass. There's a spring under it. You get down below the lip and you're out of the wind. The ground gives back its heat at night. Warm as a hearth, some nights."

"Is that where you slept, after—" She could not say it.

"Some nights." He said it without weight. "You learn what the land's willing to give. Most of the time it's not much. But it's never nothing."

She held that in her chest like a smooth stone.

Near dusk they hid in a dry ditch under a thorn hedge while two riders passed within a hundred yards. Elara lay with her face in the crook of her arm, breathing through her mouth, and felt Kael's hand close around her wrist. Not to stop her—she was not moving—but to hold her. The bracelet rustled faintly against his thumb. The hoofbeats faded into the wind, and the wind took them away.

He did not say "we're safe." She had noticed that. He never said "safe." He said "we're all right" or "they've moved on" or, once, in the raw hour before dawn, "I think they missed us." It was scrupulous. He would not give her more hope than he could count out, like rations. But he would give her all of that.

They walked through the dusk and into the night, the moon up, the ground dry, the heather rolling in silver and black like a vanished sea. She understood, suddenly, why he had walked east. The moors remembered the sea.

He stopped in the deep of the night at a subtle change in the wind she would not have noticed, and said, "Here." A shepherd's shelter: three walls of dry stone, a roof of branches and turf collapsed at one end. It was four degrees warmer inside. She felt it on her face like a blessing.

He got a fire going with Bess's flint and steel, grass tinder catching on the third strike. A flame no bigger than her thumb, fed twig by twig until it had the courage to eat larger branches. The stone walls turned orange. He set the turnips to roast in the embers and they ate them hot, the first hot food since Gorse's stew. She burned her fingers and did not care.

"Slow," Kael said.

"Water, I'm not a horse. Food, I'm allowed to be a little of one."

He looked at her. The firelight found the hollows under his cheekbones.

She laughed. It came out rusty, a hand-crank turned for the first time in months, and it surprised her so much she laughed again, smaller and wetter.

"I don't know why I'm laughing."

"I do. You're still walking."

She looked at her hands in the firelight. The nails were broken. Dirt in the creases. A blister on her palm from the bundle strap. Calluses beginning, small and painful, at the bases of her fingers.

"They'll get harder," Kael said. "The skin learns."

"Kael. What are you afraid of?"

He stirred the embers for so long she thought he would not answer. Then he said, "That I'll stop. Not because I want to. The day after the flogging, the day I lay in the heather and thought about not getting up—that was my limit. I had one day's worth of walking left in me, and I spent it, and then I found the cache, and I spent that too, and there was nothing left but the idea of you. And ideas don't weigh much, but they're stronger than legs."

He looked into the dark beyond the fire, the way she had looked out the east tower window when she lived in a different body.

"I'm afraid I'll spend my last day's worth and there won't be an idea left strong enough to carry me. But so far there's always been one."

She reached across the fire and took his hand. The bracelet scraped against his wrist.

"There'll always be one," she said. "I'll be right here. I'm an idea you can carry."

His hand closed over hers. He smiled. It was the first true smile since the village.

"Then I'll keep walking."

She dreamed of the sea. In the dream she stood in the shallows, and Kael was carrying her across the water, and she could see the cottage on the shore, the door standing open, the shelf with the book on it, the garden where heather bloomed. She tried to tell him—Kael, it's there, it's right there—

She woke with his arm around her, the fire dead, the wind thinning toward dawn. He was already awake.

"We should walk."

"Kael—"

"I know," he said. "I dreamed it too."

The fever day—she would think of it later as the fever day, though she could not have said which day it was or how many came before or after—the moor turned against them. A cold wet wind rose at midmorning, carrying rain in fits that never quite soaked through the cloak. The path turned to sucking mire. Storm laid his ears back at nothing. Her ankle, the one she had twisted leaving Thornwood, began to ache again. She did not tell him. There was nothing to be done, and telling him would only add a weight he could not carry. She watched the ground and put her foot down carefully, stone to stone, and told her ankle it could either come with her or be left behind.

They crossed the first river at dusk.

She saw it before she heard it, a wide flash of gray in the dying light, and her heart knocked against her ribs. The rivers. Beyond them were villages, work, food. She had held the promise of it for two days like a coin.

He led her upstream, looking for a crossing. "Ford's probably a mile that way, but tracks have eyes." He found a place where the river widened over a bed of stones, slow enough to read the bottom. He unbuckled Storm's girth, carried the saddle and bundle across on his shoulders, and came back for her.

"Cold," he said. "Up to your thighs. Take your boots off."

She unlaced her boots and hung them around her neck, tied her stockings into the bundle. She waded in barefoot, and the breath left her body in one hard rush. The water was beyond cold, a cold that gripped her bones and shot up through her chest. Kael was beside her, his hand under her elbow, and they moved together through the current that pulled at their calves, their thighs, the hem of her habit dragging like lead.

"Don't think," he said. "Just put the next foot down."

She put the next foot down. The stones were slick. The water pulled her. His hand was steady.

The water shallowed. The far bank came up under her feet, and Kael drew her up out of the river, water streaming from her clothes, and she stood on the far bank dripping and laughing, not knowing why, not caring.

He was laughing too. A quiet, breathless sound, as rusty as hers. They stood in the wet grass, holding each other's wrists, and let the water run off them.

"We made the river," she said.

"We made the river."

He looked back across the water at the dark land they had left. Then at the dark land ahead, indistinguishable in the moonlight.

"Beyond this there's another. A bigger one, maybe. I remember the map in your father's study. The first river, then the second, and then—" He shrugged. "I never got past the second. I'd always planned to. I'd look at the map and think, past the second river, there. That's where I'd go, if I ever went anywhere."

"Where is it? Past the second river."

He looked at her. Moonlight caught the water still streaming from his beard.

"I never gave it a name. I thought if I gave it a name, it would be real, and I couldn't stand the way it felt to want something real."

She understood. The cottage by the sea was not a place to him. It was a shape he had learned to want the way a man in a dungeon learns to want sunlight—not because he will see it, but because wanting it is the only thing that keeps the dark from filling him up.

She let go of his wrist and put her hand on his chest, over the old scar. He stood very still. She felt his heart move under her palm.

"Give it a name," she said. "The place past the second river. Give it a name so I can walk toward it."

He was silent. The river talked to itself behind them. The wind moved across the new country, the land past the first river, and she thought: this is the whole thing, this moment, wet and cold and alive on the bank of a river with his heart under my hand.

"Home," Kael said. The word came out rough, like he had to pull it from deep in his chest. "Past the second river, there's home. That's the name of it."

She stood very still. His heart moved under her palm.

"Home," she said. The word tasted like salt, like the sea, like the grit of the turnip skins. "Then that's where we're going. That's where we walk to."

He reached up and covered her hand with his own, pressing it against his chest. Water dripped from his beard. His eyes in the moonlight were bright, and she thought he might be crying, or she might be crying, or the river was still on both their faces and would not let her tell the difference.

"Home," he said again, quieter, as if testing whether the word would hold. It held. It held against the sound of the river, against the wind, against the two days behind them and the riders somewhere in the dark, held like a stone placed carefully in a seam, like a wall that would stand.

She let him keep the word. She kept it too, in her chest beside the smooth stone of it's never nothing, and she thought: I am still walking. We are still walking. Toward home.

They picked up their boots and their bundle and Storm's reins, and they walked on into the dark, east, past the first river, toward the second, carrying the name between them like a flame cupped in the hands against the wind.

chapters.name: Cottage and Children
chapters.content:
The fifth night found the wreck of a chapel. It stood alone in a fold of the moor, its roof gone, its tower cracked like a dry bone. Dusk had turned the heather the color of rust, and the wind picked through the empty windows as if it had business there. Kael stopped at the edge of the standing wall and read the place the way he read every place now—for the pocket, the seam, the story the wind told about who had been through last.

"Empty," Elara said.

"Empty's not safe," he answered. "Empty only means nothing's here yet."

They came through the long grass. The door hung off a single hinge in the west wall, and beyond it the nave lay open to the sky, scattered with fallen stones and a briar that had grown through the flagstones and swallowed the altar. A stone bird, or a piece of one, clung to the broken window arch. The whole place had the look of a body left so long in the heather that the land had begun to forget it.
