Cook frowned into her pot. "The first one smiled all the time. Smiled and laughed and sang, going about the house. And look what came of it." The servants' hall considered, in a silence of some duration, what had come of it. "A woman doesn't stop smiling for nothing," said Cook.

"Cursed," breathed the scullery girl, in the tone of one offering the only possible explanation. "She's cursed. That's why the master's away so much."

The footman said he had seen her on the east stair at three in the morning, barefoot, and the stairs had not creaked. "They creak for me," he said, with the air of a man who has been personally wronged. "Seven, nineteen, twenty-four. They creak for everyone. They did not creak for her."

Mrs. Venn came into the room at that moment, as she always came into such rooms at such moments, as if summoned by indiscretion, and the whispers died like flies at the first frost. She said nothing. She had watched three brides, and this one was not like the others. The first had cried for a month. The second had wept in private. This one did not weep at all, and Mrs. Venn, who believed in the ledger of the household and in little else, thought that a woman who did not grieve had simply hammered the door shut. And doors, in her thirty years of service, never stayed shut forever.

---

Lord Vexford told her at breakfast, a week after the dinner, that he would ride out with Halworth for the partridge.

"Halworth has the best shooting in the county," he said, reading a letter that had come with the post. "I shall go tomorrow and return in three days, or four." He folded the letter and looked at her with the look he gave a page of accounts—even, appraising, searching for the line that did not balance. "You do not ask where I am going."

"Where are you going, my lord?"

"Halworth's shooting."

He waited. The mantel clock gave its small judgment.

"You do not ask when I shall return," he said.

"When will you return, my lord?"

"Thursday, or Friday at the latest." He set the letter down. "You ask only when you are bid. Is that compliance, or indifference?"

"I have given you what you asked for, my lord," said Elara, pouring the tea with a steady hand. "You told me you preferred a quiet wife. I have made myself quiet. It seemed the only honest use of your permission."

"Quiet is one thing," said Vexford. "Dead is another."

The word lay on the tablecloth between them. Elara felt a small, cold pulse of satisfaction that he, not she, had brought it into the room, and so she would not have to. "I am not dead, my lord. I run your house; it runs well. I keep your accounts; they balance. The dead do not keep accounts."

"And what do you do when the accounts are kept?"

"I wait."

"For what?"

"For you to return, my lord, or to tell me what else you require. Those are the only two doors you have left open, and I do not presume to open others."

It was a speech that might have been read as humility. Vexford was silent a moment. Then he said, "See that the lamp is lit in the study window. I prefer to see it from the road."

"I will, my lord."

He went the next afternoon with a groom and two dogs. Elara stood at the morning-room window and watched the horsemen take the road until they were small as her thumbnail and then gone. The house settled around her like a held breath released. She had not known she was braced until the brace was gone. Her shoulders came down from her ears. That night the space in the bed beside her was enormous, and cold, and hers.

The lamp burned in the study window until dawn.

It became a pattern. That was the terrible gift of time: it taught every object its own shape, and the shape of Blackmoor Hall was the shape of a departing horseman. October was the partridge. November was the hunts, the meets at crossroad inns, the long nights at other men's tables. In December he went east to look at a horse that was supposed to be the fastest in three counties, and came back without it and in a temper that lasted until he left again. He visited neighbors. He sat on committees. He had business at the port that required a day and then a day more. Each departure followed the same ritual: his instructions, the request for the lamp, her answer. And she lit it, and she kept it burning, and on the nights he came to her bed she counted heartbeats as she had counted lashes, and in the morning he was gone, and the count was all she remembered.

He came home once and stood in the drawing-room doorway, in his traveling coat, and watched her at the accounts. "You have made the house run so well," he said, "that it does not appear to need me."

"It is your house, my lord. It would not run at all without your name above the door."

"My name," he repeated, and went up to change. When he came down, he was dressed for riding out again.

Once, returning from the market town, he brought her a book. It was bound in brown leather—a history of the county, with maps—the sort of thing a man buys when he must bring a wife something and has never noticed what she reads. He set it down at dinner with the air of a man laying a bet. "For the library. I thought you might have use of it."

"Thank you, my lord." She opened it. The endpapers were marbled, the plates foxed, the corners sharp as though the pages had never been turned. "It is very kind."

"I have never seen you read," he said.

"Nor will you, my lord, if you bring me books from the county library." He looked up sharply, and she met his eyes, and a silence passed between them in which she considered whether she had said too much and decided she did not greatly care. Then the mask returned, the door went shut, and she added, "But I will value it above any other book in the house. You chose it for me. That is worth more than the reading."

He did not ask her again. She took the book to the east tower that night, not to read but to find the maps, and she laid her forefinger along the eastern coast and followed it down until she reached the place where the cliffs stood over the sea and the mapmaker had written, in a plain hand, *Unsurveyed*. She said the harbor names to the cold glass—Coldwell, Blackwater, Saltcombe, Rook's Reach—and then the invented names of the places she and Kael had meant to reach, and then, once, inside her skull, his name, like a key turning in a lock.

The key itself was warm against her sternum. Vexford had seen the ribbon. He had touched it. He had accepted the lie that it was a keepsake from her mother. He had not seen the key, and she had never once felt the impulse to show it to him. What it opened she still did not know. Perhaps nothing. Perhaps she had stolen it simply to cast a vote about doors, and the only door that had mattered had been shut a year ago and could not be reopened by any key the world contained.

---

The snow came in January, while he was away at Marney's. It began in the evening, small stings against the glass, and by the time she climbed the east tower the moors were white to the dark line of the wall.

She stood at the rippled window with her palms flat on the cold sill and watched it fall the way it had fallen that first winter at Thornwood, when she had gone to the stable and found him there. The memory came without her permission, preserved in the exactness of just those moments she could not have: the smell of hay and warm horse, the snow drifting through the open door, his hands moving over Storm's mane as if the animal were precious, the way he had listened while she spoke her fear of a man whose name she had not then had any right to speak. Lord Vexford. She had been afraid of him then. Now she was Lady Vexford, and the fear had been the only thing she had to look forward to, and it had not even come to her properly in the end. The thing she had feared was a reasonable man who brought her books she could not read and asked her, once, in the dark, *Who are you, then?* And she had not known, and did not know, and would not know, because the only answer she had ever possessed was sleeping at the bottom of a black sea.

Her wrist moved in the sleeve as she pressed against the sill, and something fell.

It was small: a crescent of dried grass, loosened at last from the bracelet by the months of wearing and the weather and the slow entropy of anything a man makes with his hands. She caught it before it reached the floor. She held it in her palm—a curl of pale dead grass, one dark hair, a fragment of the only thing in the world that was hers and his. She looked at it for a long time.

*Everything a man makes with his hands breaks. That doesn't mean he shouldn't make it.*

She had not wept since the cliff. She had not wept in the chapel or in the carriage or in the strange bed, and she did not weep now. She closed her hand over the fragment. It could not be braided back; it could not be mended. It was the size of the vow she had made to keep him alive inside her, and the vow was wearing out, too. She could not hold it without breaking it.

She put the fragment between her lips.

It tasted of dust. It tasted of nothing at all. She swallowed, and felt it go down like a cinder, and touched the bracelet where it lay against her wrist—thinner than it had been in the summer, full of gaps where his hair had been.

"I am still wearing it," she said to the empty tower. And then, to the snow, to the moors, to the dark line of the sea in the north: "I am still wearing it."

The snow fell. The lamp burned in the study window because she had lit it and would light it again. The household continued.

---

By the turn of the year, the county had agreed on her. The new Lady Vexford was a perfect mistress of Blackmoor Hall: accounts balanced, staff disciplined, dinners immaculate. She was spoken of at other tables as a model of wifely governance, and it was remarked, with a little shrug, that she was quiet—"You know how these northern girls are"—and that she never smiled, and the story, passed hand to hand, grew smooth as a stone in a stream.

Lord Vexford was away more than he was home, and Elara was grateful for his absence. Grateful was the word she used, in the small arithmetic she still kept. She was grateful the way a held breath is grateful for the loosening of the chest, the way a woman with one coat on a cold road is grateful for the walking.

At night, in the east tower, she pressed her palms to the cold glass and recited the names, and the moors below her were white and empty and full of the only company she had ever kept. In the morning the lamp was taken down from the study window, the household woke to its order, and she put on the gray gown and went down to run the perfect house that was, in every particular, a tomb. She was the candle left burning in its window, and there was nobody left on the road to see.

Two things she kept: the key, warm against her sternum, and the bracelet, thinning against her wrist. And inside her, in the dark of her body, one small crescent of dried grass and a strand of hair, gone down like a spark, and still glowing.

The moors waited. They were in no hurry. They had waited for her before she was born, and they would wait for her long after she was dead—and she was not dead, not yet. She was only a bride who did not smile, the perfect mistress of the perfect house, walking the cold halls at night like a ghost.

chapters.name: The Walking Ghost
chapters.content:
# Chapter 35: The Walking Ghost

The lamp had been their only ritual, and it ended without ceremony.

For months Elara had lit it in the study window whenever Vexford rode out, and kept it burning until dawn or until he came. He had asked for it once; she had never needed to be asked again. It was a contract, like everything between them. Then in the first thaw of February he came home from Marney's town and did not look at the window, and the following week he rode away and did not ask, and Elara lit the lamp anyway, out of habit — a lighthouse keeper with no ship.

She might have gone on that way. But the house knew before she did; houses always know. The young maid's voice dropped when the master's name came up. Cook looked at the ceiling. One afternoon, gathering his laundry, Elara found a handkerchief in his riding coat — cambric, finer than her own, embroidered at the corner with a D in moss-green thread. She studied it as she would study a bill, put it back where she found it, exact to the inch, and went up to the east tower.

She stood at the rippled window a long time, waiting for what she had been told all her life she would feel. She had never held a rival before. She pressed her hands to the cold sill and searched the flat gray country of herself for jealousy, and found none. She searched for anger. There was no anger. Not even surprise. The glass showed her own face, thin and white and composed, and behind it the moors, and the two were the same picture.

That evening Mrs. Venn found her in the linen room and delivered the news the way she delivered soiled napkins — an item, an inventory. The master kept a woman in Marney's town. A widow. Mrs. Grace Deane, relict of a wool factor. Thirty years of service had taught Mrs. Venn to speak before the servants' hall did, where the rumor was already the shape of the evening's entertainment.

"Thank you, Mrs. Venn," Elara said. "A widow in Marney's town is not a household matter."

Mrs. Venn stood a moment. "No, my lady." "You'll do" had been her verdict; it hung in the air unrevised.

"Does she sing, Mrs. Venn?"

The question surprised them both. Mrs. Venn considered it with the gravity of a woman who had watched three brides come to Blackmoor Hall. "I believe the master has not asked her to."

"Then I hope she is very quiet," Elara said, "and that she does not require the lamp."

Mrs. Venn left. Elara let the sheet fall and stood in the center of the room, waiting for the grief that did not come, and was afraid of how little she felt it.

That night Vexford came to her bed, and she lay beneath him counting heartbeats, and afterward he said, "You must have heard. About Deane."

"Yes."

"You might have said something."

"What would you have me say, my lord? You are a reasonable man. You told me you preferred a quiet wife. I have made myself quiet. It seemed the only honest use of your permission."

"There is a kind of quiet," he said, "that is a door."

"Then I hope the door holds," she said, "for your sake."

He did not understand her, and she did not clarify, and in the dark she watched the ceiling and felt the old key warm against her sternum and did not once speak Kael's name aloud.

Before the widow came to dinner, a letter arrived from Thornwood. Margaret wrote in her small, precise hand — four pages of weather and repairs and the vexation of a new maid — and at the end, as if the ink had tired: The county says you never smile. Your father says nothing, which is the same as saying it is settled. People are beginning to ask what you are thinking.

Elara read the words twice. She had known, when she walked backward to her father on the cliff, that she would never be loved or understood. She had not known her mother would write to her as to a stranger — as if Margaret had never stood at a locked window, as if the sea-glass ring had never been pressed into her palm by a trembling hand on her sixteenth birthday.

She did not answer the question. She answered the letter: the house was well, the accounts balanced, the master in good health and often from home. She sealed it with Blackmoor's gray wax and felt the bright-worn key against her sternum, and wondered what it would take to write a letter that told the truth.

The mistress was presented in April. Not formally — no announcement, no carriage. Vexford was a ledger-reader and did not publish his accounts. But the widow was brought to dinner on a wet Tuesday, with a brother-in-law as a fading chaperone, and Elara served her soup.

Mrs. Deane was younger than Elara had expected, with auburn hair and a low, warm laugh that carried through the dining room like a songbird. She was not cruel and not stupid, and she looked at Elara with an uncertainty that was almost sympathy. She had been told, perhaps, that the lady of the house was cold; she had not been told it was winter.

"My lady," Mrs. Deane said over the fish, "your house is beautiful."

"Thank you." Elara's voice was the voice she used in every room of the house: precise, flat, a sheet smoothed by a hand.

"You must have worked very hard."

"I keep the accounts, Mrs. Deane. The house keeps itself."

Vexford watched them the way a man watches two ledgers he expects to balance. Mrs. Deane tried again, with the doggedness of a woman who has decided to be kind. "I hope you will come to Marney's town sometime. Do you sing, my lady?"

"No," Elara said, "I have never sung."

She saw the flicker of pity in the widow's face — pity from the woman sleeping in her husband's bed — and the sensation was so distant she had to name it to be sure it was herself. Not jealousy. Not anger. It was the feeling of a window watched from inside, of rain on the glass.

The dinner concluded. Elara withdrew through the cold corridors and climbed the east stairs — seven, nineteen, twenty-four, silent for her, creaking for everyone — and stood at the tower window as Vexford walked the widow to her carriage and watched until it was a speck on the road. She felt nothing. She had expected, perhaps, a small sharp satisfaction — the widow in her husband's bed meant the door of her own would close. But the relief, if it was relief, was so faint she could not be certain it was hers. It was like the remembered warmth of a fire long out.

"Coldwell," she said to the dark. "Blackwater. Saltcombe. Rook's Reach."

The names lay on the air and sank. The moors were a black sea under the moon. Somewhere out there, in the green country of memory, a man walked beside her and named the unnameable place home. She had locked the door behind her when she walked backward to her father on the cliff. She did not open it now. She only stood in the tower and let the names go down like stones into well water, and the key lay warm against her sternum, and she did not weep. She had not wept since the cliff, and she was afraid — not that the tears would come, but that they had gone out of her forever, like a spring that had stopped.

Spring came to the moors in its slow peasant way. The snow left the high ground. The heather greened, and the gray land grew a thin beard that from the tower window looked like patience. Elara watched it the way other women watched a clock. The moors had become her company — vast, empty, unfurnished, as gray as she was, as endless as the minutes. She learned their weather: how the cloud shadows moved across them like hands turning pages, how the light changed at the hour she used to meet Kael in the library, how the road to the east held a thread of silver after rain. And she learned them as she had learned the house, walking them in memory until they were a second country inside her. Here the farmyard where Kael had taken turnips and left a copper in the trough; here the river where he had carried the saddle, then the bundle, then her; here the ruined chapel where they built the cottage aloud — door and table and green-stone hearth and children with his steady hands. The visible land gave up no trace of any of it. The moors kept their secrets as completely as she kept hers, and she loved them for that, hated them for that, and told no one.

Below stairs in April the story changed shape. It was not the first time the master had kept a woman away from home. The footman remembered the first wife's years — the silk scarf from the port, the lady's tears, the master's silence. The scullery girl asked if the new lady wept in private as the second wife had done. Mrs. Venn said nothing. The new lady had not wept at her wedding, and she had not wept when the widow came to table; but she lit the lamp every night for a man who no longer asked for it. Mrs. Venn could not say what the lady was waiting for, and that was the trouble with the lady. She was waiting, and no one could tell for what.

Through May and into June, Elara kept the accounts and they balanced. She grew thinner, the way a held note grows faint, and her ankle throbbed in the damp, and she counted the beats of the pain as she had once counted the lashes, because it was a number and numbers did not lie. She slept in the hour before dawn, if at all. In the tower she kept the county history open on the chair — the one Vexford had brought her as a man buys a wife a gift without looking at her — her forefinger laid along the eastern coast where the mapmaker had written Unsurveyed, and beyond it the sea.

One evening in early June a small thing fell from her wrist: a crescent of dried grass and one dark hair, loosened from the bracelet at last. She caught it before it touched the floor, held it in her palm — a thing smaller than a fingernail, the last craft of a man who had said, "Everything a man makes with his hands breaks. That doesn't mean he shouldn't make it." She put it between her lips. It tasted of dust and of nothing, and she swallowed, and it went down like a spark, and she touched the bracelet — thinner now, full of gaps, a garland that would not outlast the year.

"I am still wearing it," she said to the tower, and then to the moors, and then to the dark line of the sea. "I am still wearing it."

At midsummer the county came to Blackmoor Hall for the feasting — Lady Pritcham first, as she was everywhere, her small eyes missing nothing. The widow was not of the company; Vexford kept his ledgers separate. But the story of the bride who never smiled had grown smooth as a stone in a stream, and Lady Pritcham wore it like a jewel.

"My lady," she said in the garden, where the roses had not survived Elara's management, "you have been married a full year, and I have never once seen you smile."

"Then the year has been a success," Elara said, "for that is exactly what you expected of me."

Lady Pritcham laughed. "You are clever. Your mother wrote that you were headstrong. She did not write that you were clever."

"My mother writes what the post requires."

"And are you happy, my lady?"

It was the first time anyone had asked directly. Elara considered it as she would consider an invoice. "I am the mistress of Blackmoor Hall. The house runs well. The accounts balance. I have a view of the moors from the east tower, and no one above me but the sky. What would you call happy, Lady Pritcham?"

"I should call it something warmer than that."

"Then I am sorry for you," Elara said, "for you will find nothing warmer than that in me."

Lady Pritcham looked at her a long moment. "No," she said, "I don't suppose we shall. But we shall all go on looking, shan't we? That is what people do with a walking ghost."

The word fell between them. Elara did not flinch. "It is a good phrase. You must use it when you tell the story."

"Oh, I shall," said Lady Pritcham. And she did.

On the longest day of the year, the first year of her marriage closed. Her father wrote nothing — her father never wrote. He had promised her the affair would be forgotten, and he had kept his word; silence was the only coin he had ever paid her willingly. She wore his stolen key against her breast and wondered whether he had found it gone — whether a man who kept accounts of obedience would count a missing key among his losses, or whether he had simply aged another year in the empty house, forgetting, as men forget, what they have locked away.

The lamp burned in the study window that night, though no one was on the road to see it. She stood in the east tower with the summer moors lying below in their green, the heather not yet bloomed — it would come in July, purple and alive, a violent bloom over empty land. Somewhere beyond the edge of the map she had traced so often, the sea went on being the last door left. She pressed her palms to the glass and recited the harbor names, then the invented names of places they meant to reach, and then, once, inside her skull, she turned Kael's name like a key in a lock.

She had not wept since the cliff. She had not smiled since the wedding. She was the perfect mistress of Blackmoor Hall, and she was a walking ghost, and when she looked at the moors she saw herself — gray, endless, patient — and she did not know yet how long she could go on being the pane of glass between the world and the sea.

Below, in the servants' hall, the young maid said she was cursed. Mrs. Venn said nothing. She had watched three brides come to Blackmoor Hall, and she had said of this one: you'll do. But she knew, with the certainty of thirty years, that a woman who does not grieve has hammered the door shut, and that doors never stay shut forever.

The lamp burned on. The moors held their silence. And the sea, out of sight beyond the edge of the land, went on being the last door left — and it was open.

chapters.name: The East Tower Window
chapters.content:
After the longest day the heather came. It rose out of the moors like a slow tide, first in the hollows where water drained, then up the low slopes, until the eastward land from the tower window lay under a purple so deep it read as black in the failing light—a second sea lying where the earth had been. By day the bloom was a brazen thing, humming with bees, heavy with its own perfume; the tower window smelled of honey and dust. At dusk the color pooled and spread, and where it reached the horizon it lost itself in a last purple band of light, and the moors seemed to tip into the sky. Elara stood at the glass and watched it bloom, and felt the familiar nothing, and knew that the nothing was not a hole in her but a door kept shut. The world went on being alive without her permission. The heather did not ask whether she was glad or grieving; it simply bloomed, as he had once said the sea was—no wall, no gate, no master.

She was thinner now. It had begun without a decision, the way a held note fades without deciding to. She sat at the long table, took up the spoon, put it down, watched the candle, and when the maid cleared the plates she had eaten the bread and forgotten the rest. She had starved herself once, deliberately, in the hollow days at Thornwood, and she knew the shape of that hunger. This was different. This was not refusing the world. This was forgetting that it had been offered.

The gray gown had been taken in at the waist in August, and again in October. The wedding ring, too large from the first day, turned on her finger; she worked it over the knuckle without soap and studied the pale band beneath where her mother's ring had been. She slept in the hour before dawn, if at all, counting the cracks in the carved ceiling as she had once counted lashes; the ceiling never ran out. Her ankle throbbed when the damp came in, and she counted its beats. A number did not lie.

Every night she climbed to the tower. The stairs knew her now—the seventh, nineteenth, and twenty-fourth treads, which creaked for everyone, did not creak for her, as if her weight had already been subtracted from the house. She went barefoot and left no candle. She stood at the window until the glass grew cold, and the moors grew dark, and the sea, out of sight, went on breathing.

Mrs. Venn noticed everything; that was what she was paid for. With the master away, she kept the observation in the ledger of herself, and one evening when the heather was browning she carried a bowl of broth up the east tower stairs.

"Your ladyship will not keep body on bread and candle ends."

Elara turned from the window. "I am not hungry, Mrs. Venn."

"That was not what I said."

Elara took the bowl; it steamed between them, smelling of the good kitchen, of the world continuing.

"You spend a great deal of time looking east."

"The view is a fine one."

"It is." The housekeeper watched the moors. "The first mistress looked west, toward the gardens. The east is a hungry direction, my lady. Nothing comes from it but the sea."

Elara said nothing. Mrs. Venn left. The broth sat on the sill until it skinned over, and Elara poured it into the dark.

Vexford came home for a single night in the yellowing of the leaves. He did not come to her bed; he came to her table and watched her move the food around her plate.

"You were thinner in the summer," he said. "You are thinner now."

"It is the turning of the year, my lord."

"It is that you do not eat." He waited; she offered nothing. "Mrs. Deane sends her regards. She finds you very quiet and very beautiful, and she is sorry for you."

The widow's pity, posted through her husband's mouth, tasted of nothing at all. "Kind of her. I hope the season finds her well."

"You might say more."

"I have nothing more, my lord. I have given you everything I have."

"You are disappearing," he said. "I am not sure you are doing it on purpose, and I am not sure it matters."

"It does not matter. I run your house; it runs well."

She ate a bite of bread. He watched her chew. He left in the morning, and the lamp burned in the study window all night though he had not asked for it and was not on the road to see.

The moors would not let her alone. The heather was a sea, and the sea was memory, and memory was a door she had sworn shut, but the window was a pane of glass and the world on the other side would not stop moving. At night, in the tower, she let herself replay it in order, the way she ran the accounts—a ledger, a debt rendered fair.

Sometimes the wind came off the sea and moved across the heather in long swells until she could not tell where the land ended and the water began, could not tell whether the sound in her ears was the surf miles off or the beating of her own tired blood. It did not matter. Both said the same word, if she listened long enough.

The first time: a frost-rimed window at Thornwood, and a man she had never seen gentling a stallion that had kicked two grooms, his hands moving over the animal's neck with a quiet authority that lodged in her chest like a splinter of light.

The stable, a bitter winter morning, a dying mare the other grooms had abandoned. He had sat with the animal, murmuring, and Elara had watched a whole tenderness pass from his hands into its neck—reverence no man of her class had ever shown to anything—and had understood that she had never once been looked at that way, and would have given everything she owned to be, for a moment.

The library, dust motes, his mouth laboring over a word. She had taught him to read, but he had taught her that a man who wanted the names of things could be trusted with the things themselves.

The doorframe in the first snow. His hand brushing hers, meaning nothing, meaning everything. She had carried that touch into the dark the way a candle carries its flame.

The hunting lodge, rain on the roof, her own voice: "I do not want your protection. I want you." The kiss that was a dam breaking.

The courtyard at dawn, and the lash, and his silence. Twenty strikes. She had counted them from her bedchamber with her hands flat against the stone, willing the blows into her own body. He had looked at her once, and then at Martha, understanding everything, and had made no sound, and when they cut him down he had walked east with his back in ribbons and had not looked back.

The moonless night before her wedding. The hidden stair behind the carved rose, the stillroom door, Bess's hand in the dark, Storm's warm breath in the dark. She had left the wedding dress on its stand like a sleeping woman and had not looked back.

The flight north and inland. A river crossed at dusk, the saddle, the bundle, then her weight on his back through the dark water.

The ruined chapel on the fifth night, the cottage built aloud: a door, a table, a green-stone hearth, a shelf for the sea book, a garden, children with his steady hands and her sharp eyes. They had built it so carefully that it stood somewhere still, real and roofed, waiting.

The torches on the hills at dawn. The second river in the dark, chest-deep, and on the far bank he released Storm with a slap; the horse walked north along the bank. East, then, to a sea that had no harbor. Coldwell. Blackwater. Saltcombe. Rook's Reach. None of the names answered, and the last door had been the sea.

Raven's Point. The wind. Her father's voice offering to forget. Kael's voice refusing to be kept, refusing to be forgiven for her sake. He had stepped backward into the void and fallen in silence, watching her, into the black sea. She had counted heartbeats on the ride home as she had counted lashes, as she would count cracks and lamps and the beats of her ankle. A number did not lie.

She could watch it now without weeping. She had said once that if she began she would not stop, so she had never begun, and now she feared the spring had gone dry in her forever—not that the tears would come, but that they had gone out of her, like a spring that had stopped. But something else moved in her now, something that was not grief and not yet hope. A correction of direction.

For a year she had thought of Raven's Point as the place where she had lost him. But he had not been taken there; he had gone there, walking backward, watching her, smiling through the falling air. The place where he had left the world was the only place in the world that still held him. There was no grave, no recovered body, no stone. Thornwood kept his absence in an empty chair; the moors kept the memory of a man walking east, barefoot and shirtless. But the point kept the last of him—the air above the water, the place his breath had gone through. If anywhere in the world still held him, it was there.

She began to think of it as a place she might walk to. She had the county history's maps, her finger worn to the margin where the mapmaker had written Unsurveyed. She had the reckoning: three hours across the moors, east and north, until the ground fell away and the sea opened. She was not thinking of dying. It mattered to be precise: the sea was not going to take her. She was going to stand in the air that had received him, and breathe him in, and be, for one hour, near. The way she had swallowed the fragments. The way she kept his name in her skull. Near.

One evening, undressing, a third crescent fell from the bracelet—a curl of dried grass, one dark hair—and she caught it out of the air the way she would have caught a falling glass. She stood in her shift and looked at it: the last true things his hands had made. She had said the garland would not outlast the year, and it would not. She put the fragment to her lips; it went down like a spark, and she said to the empty tower, to the dark line of the sea beyond the moors, "I am still wearing it."

The bracelet was all gaps now. She could count the surviving strands the way she counted cracks; it sat against her wrist like a memory of a memory, and beneath it her skin had gone pale, a second ring where the grass had been.

She understood now what the keeping was for. It had never been the grass. It was the swallowing, the carrying, the turning of him into the interior country of herself, fragment by fragment, until nothing was left of the garland and everything was left of him. A number did not lie, but neither did a swallowed spark. She was wearing him now the way the sea wears a river—taken in, carried, invisible, and still there.

Autumn deepened into winter. The heather died to brown, and the moors went the color of a held breath, and snow came down and made a white sea of everything, unmarked but for the wind. Elara ran Blackmoor Hall with a precision that seemed to rise from the ground like frost. The walking ghost, the county said, had grown thinner still; Lady Pritcham added that the bride was sometimes seen at the east tower window, standing so still that the servants crossed themselves.

Below stairs the words had settled into a story. The lady was cursed; the master was never home; the house would not thrive. The scullery girl crossed herself when she passed the east stair. The footman said the new lady was not dying—the dead were peaceful—she was being drawn, the way a needle is drawn to the pole, only no one could see the hand holding the magnet.

Mrs. Venn saw the trays return untouched. She saw the lamp lit every night for a man who no longer asked. She said nothing, but she thought that grief hammered behind a door would not stay shut forever, and that the lady had never been waiting for the master at all. What the lady was waiting for, Mrs. Venn could not say; that, she decided, was the trouble with the lady. She was waiting, and no one could tell for what.

Elara knew. She knew the way a locked door knows its key.

The heather would come again in July, purple and violent over the empty land, and before the bloom, at the turn of the year's longest days, would come the anniversary—the season of his death and of her burial in white, the two catastrophes tangled in the same green month. She would go then. East, three hours, across the moors, to the place where the land fell away and the sea opened and the last door stood open. Not to die. To be near him. If the difference meant something to her—and it did—she would hold it in her hands the way she held the stolen key against her sternum, the key taken from a man who had tried to lock the whole world against her. She had been tired of doors shut in her face. This one was open. It had always been open.

She rehearsed the route the way she rehearsed a dinner menu, course by course. The service door, the stable yard at the hour the grooms took their meal, then the moors east and north. If the ankle failed, the ankle would fail; she had walked on worse. She would need her strength, and so, on certain days, she began to eat a little more, and to sleep when sleep came, hoarding her body the way a miser hoards coin, because a journey requires a body and she had nearly spent hers.

At the window in the last of the light, she pressed her palms to the cold glass. The lamp burned behind her, lit for a man who was not on the road. The moors lay white under the failing sky. Beyond the edge of the land, out of sight, the sea went on being the last door left—and it was open.

She said his name aloud, once, into the glass. It did not dissolve into a dark that gave nothing back, the way it had on the night before her wedding. It came back to her off the cold pane, or seemed to, as if the moors had been holding it all this time, waiting to give it to her.

"I am coming," she said. "Not to the sea. To you."

And she stood there, keeping it, until the light was gone and the east was only dark, and the last door, out of sight beyond the edge of the land, went on being open, patient as the tide.

chapters.name: The Anniversary
chapters.content:
The anniversary came with the heather beginning, in the long green days at the turn of the year. The moors had gone from winter gray to spring green to the first deep bruise of purple rising along the edges of the land, and the east tower window stood open for the first time in months. The air moved through it warm and heavy with the beginning of honey. Elara stood at the glass and pressed her palms to the sill and looked out at the country she had rehearsed all winter.

Three hours. She had said it to herself so often it had worn a path in her skull, the way water wears a stone. The service door. The stable yard at the hour the grooms took their meal. Then the moors east and north, across the shallow valley, along the spine of the ridge where the wind never quite stopped, down past the shepherd's hut whose roof had fallen in the autumn. And then the land would tip, and the sea would open.

This was not the flight. She understood that with a clarity that felt like cold water. On the flight she had been running from something with everything she had loved at her side. This was a walk to something, alone, and what she was walking to was not a place but a body of air. He had stepped backward into it. It had received him. It was still there, waiting, patient as the tide.

The household had settled into its midsummer drowsiness. Mrs. Venn conducted the morning inventory with a face like arithmetic, and Elara answered the usual questions with the usual words, and no one remarked that her voice had gone quieter, because her voice had been quiet for a year.

"Will my lady take broth at midday?"

"I will not be here at midday, Mrs. Venn."

A pause. Mrs. Venn's eyes were the gray of the moors in winter. She did not ask where her lady would be. She had learned, in thirty years of service and of watching brides come and go, that asking was a door one opened at one's own risk.

"I will keep broth against your return," she said.

Elara inclined her head. It was not a promise. It was an acknowledgment, the way one acknowledges the weather. The master was away—at Marney's town or somewhere on the road; it did not matter which. Nothing at Blackmoor Hall appeared to need him, and nothing about this day would.

She went down the back stair. The seventh, the nineteenth, the twenty-fourth—the treads that creaked for everyone did not creak for her. She moved through the house the weight of a ghost subtracted from the wood, and let herself out through the service door into the white yard.

The grooms were at their meal. The stables drowsed in the heat. A single horse turned its head as she passed, but she was not taking a horse. A horse could be followed, a theft remarked, a hoofprint read. She was going on foot, lightly, the way a rumor goes.

The sun stood at the shoulder of the sky. The first warmth of the day lay over the moors like a hand.

For the first hour she walked through country she knew from the tower: the fold of the land, the line of the dying wall, the broken gate that stood at the corner of nowhere leaning on a single hinge. She passed it and did not pause. The air was full of larks, and they rose ahead of her in fountains of song and fell back into the heather and were gone, and the silence they left was the wide, amiable silence of midsummer.

Her ankle ached within the first mile, a dull throb she counted as she counted everything. She had bound it tightly. She had walked on worse. A number does not lie, but neither does it kill you unless you choose to let it. She was not choosing. She was walking east and north, three hours, to the place where the land fell away.

She thought of the last walk she had made across this country, running and stumbling, her hand in his, the torches on the hills behind them. The memory did not hurt in the way it had once hurt. It had been handled so often it had gone smooth. It was no longer the sharp edge of loss. It was an entry in a ledger written so many times the ink had become part of the page.

She crossed the shallow valley and took the spine of the ridge. The heather here was nearer to bloom, green threaded with dark purple, buds tight and secret, holding their color closed the way she had held hers. The wind came up as the land rose and moved across the heather in waves the color of change, silver and green and the deep bruise of purple. She stopped for a moment and stood in it, and the wind pressed against her like a hand, gently, saying still here, still here, all of it still here.

A shepherd stood far off with his dog, a dark figure against the sky, but he did not hail her, and she did not hail him. The county knew her story by now, the walking ghost of Blackmoor Hall. A woman in gray crossing the moors at the turn of the year was no more remarkable than the wind.

The shepherd's hut stood where she had remembered it, the roof fallen in. She did not go near it. It belonged to the flight, and she was not flying now. She was walking. Walking had a beginning and an end and a body in it, and she was that body, and the land was that road, and the sea would be there when the land stopped. It had always been there. She had only been unable, for a long time, to walk toward it without grief. Today the grief was not absent; it was simply no longer leading. Something else had taken the bridle. It felt almost like tenderness. It felt like the last door standing open.

The sun had climbed to noon when the land began to fail.

It happened the way it happened in memory: the ridge ran out, the heather pulled back from the edge as if it too knew the drop was coming, and the world opened into sky and then into sea—a blue so deep it read as black along the horizon, glittering with the cold shattered light of northern water.

Raven's Point.

She stood where the land ended and let the salt air come to her.

Wind out of the east, tasting of the sea. She breathed it in and felt it fill the widest rooms of her. She had expected grief to be waiting here, crouched like a hawk on the cliff edge, ready to strike. But grief was not here. Or grief was here, but it had taken the shape of peace, and she could not tell where one ended and the other began.

She walked to the place. She knew it as she knew the lines of her own palm: the worn shelf of stone where the cliff had broken, the gulls' perching, the exact spot where he had stood with his back to the sea, refusing to be kept, refusing to be forgiven for her sake, watching her as he stepped backward into the void.

She stood in the exact place.

*Don't,* he had said. But he had said it for her, not for himself. He had not been refusing to fall. He had been refusing to be the reason she bent the shape of her life to save him. She understood it now as completely as she had understood it then, and the understanding no longer felt like a wound. It felt like a completed sentence.

She looked down.

The sea was a long way down. It moved below her, white at the base of the cliffs, black farther out, patient and violent at once. The waves came and went and came again, and the sound of them rose through the air and carried the rhythm of a held breath, of a heartbeat, of the counting she had done all year.

She did not jump.

She stood on the edge of the cliff where the last of him still was, and she let the salt air move into her and out of her and into her again, and she felt a strange peace settle around her shoulders like a coat placed there by a hand she could not see.

After a long time she said his name out loud, into the wind, and the wind took it and moved it over the water, and the sea kept the sound the way it keeps every sound, folded into the raft of white.

"Kael."

The name hung in the air a moment, and then the air moved on, carrying it. She watched it go.

"I have come," she said. "Not to the sea. To you."

The words went the way the name had gone, over the water, into the keeping of the air that had received him. She was not sure he heard. She was not sure it mattered. The saying of it was the completing of it, the full stop at the end of a sentence she had been writing all year.

She lifted her wrist and looked at the bracelet.

It had been a garland once, braided of his hands: dried grass and one dark hair, a thing a man makes with his hands, which breaks, because everything a man makes with his hands breaks, and that does not mean he should not make it. It had thinned through the year, fragment by fragment, and she had swallowed the fragments like sparks and felt them go on glowing inside her. What remained was a memory of a memory, a few pale strands, honest about what it had become.

The wind came up off the sea and moved through the strands, and she felt something give.

The last fragment came free—a hair, a curl of dry grass, nothing more, small as a quarter note in the ledger of the year—and she caught it out of the air the way she had caught the others, the way she would have caught a falling glass, without thinking.

She stood with it in the cup of her palm. The last true thing his hands had made.

The peace moved in her, quiet as the tide going out.

She lifted her hand to her lips and put the fragment on her tongue. It went down like a spark. It went down like a door closing, complete.

She looked at her wrist. The pale skin beneath the bracelet was bare, a second ring where the grass had been. She was wearing him now the way the sea wears a river; there was nothing left of the garland, and everything left of him.

"I am still wearing it," she said to the sea, to the air, to the place where he had left the world. It was the same thing she had said to the tower all winter, but now it was finished. She had not removed it. It had left her piece by piece, and she had kept it piece by piece, and now the keeping was complete. He was inside her. He was the sparks, the glowing, the carried river.

She stood a while longer, breathing the salt air.

She did not weep. The spring was still dry. But for the first time the dryness did not frighten her. She understood now that it was not a wound. It was a vessel poured out into something larger. The weeping had gone into the sea. The sea had it now and would keep it, patient as the tide.

She stayed until the sun had moved past noon and begun its long slope toward the west, and then she turned and began the walk home.

The walk back was harder than the walk out.

She had spent the hour at the cliff the way a wick spends an hour in a candle, steadily, unaided, burning what was left of the tallow, and now there was less of her than there had been at dawn. The ankle was a knot of counting thorns. The heat of the afternoon lay on the moors like a weight. The larks were silent. The heather held its breath.

She did not hurry. Hurrying was a form of running, and she was not running. She had come to the end of the running. She put one foot in front of the other and counted and did not lie about what the counting told her.

She had once said she would live long enough to make the rest of them sorry. She had thought she had time. She understood now that she had had exactly the time she had needed—time enough to walk to the place and stand in the air that had received him, time enough to finish the keeping, time enough to swallow the last spark and let it go on glowing inside her. The reckoning she had promised herself had arrived and passed, and it had turned out to be not war but peace, and the peace had taken her body for its own.

She came back to Blackmoor Hall as the light was going long and gold.

The service door. The back stair, which did not creak for her. The seventh, the nineteenth, the twenty-fourth—she counted them without meaning to, and the house accepted her the way it accepted the tide, without remark.

Mrs. Venn was in the passage with the broth.

She looked at Elara and said nothing. She had been looking at brides for thirty years, and she recognized a woman who had come to the end of something. It was not death, Mrs. Venn decided. It was worse and better both. It was finishing.

"The broth, my lady."

"Thank you, Mrs. Venn."

She carried it to her bedchamber and set it down and did not drink it. The gray gown she folded and laid across the chair. The key on its ribbon she did not remove. The pale ring on her wrist she looked at once in the last of the light, and then she lay down on the bed.

The window stood open to the east. The moors lay beyond it, going dark, going the color of held breath, going the color of the sea she had stood above. She could not see the sea from the bed. But she knew it was still there, out of sight beyond the edge of the land, the last door left, open, patient as the tide.

She was tired. That was the truth of it—a tiredness carried so long it no longer felt like tiredness, only like the ordinary weather of her body. She had walked three hours out and three hours back. She had stood where he had stood. She had breathed the air that had received him. She had finished the keeping of the garland, and the last spark was glowing in her, and there was nothing left to hold and nothing left to do.

She did not rise.

It was not a decision. It was more like the lamp that had burned all year in the study window for a man who was not on the road. A flame does not decide to go out. It simply reaches the end of the tallow, and the light goes on shining inward, invisible, in the new dark.

The last of the light went out of the window. The moors went to the color of memory. The sea, out of sight, went on being the last door left—and it was open.

She closed her eyes.

She was still wearing him. She would go on wearing him. It was the only vow she had left.

chapters.name: The Heather Bloom
chapters.content:
Mrs. Venn found her the next morning where she had left her, which was not the same thing as finding her asleep. The broth stood on the table, skinned over; the gray gown lay folded across the chair; and the lady lay on her back with her face turned toward the east window, her eyes open, looking at the moors as if she had been looking all night and had not yet finished.

She was not dead. Mrs. Venn had seen the dead often enough to know the difference. The dead were finished; this one was not finished. She was continuing, at a great distance, the way a candle burned down to the last of the tallow still holds the shape of a flame. It was a shape, nothing more. The light was elsewhere.

"My lady," Mrs. Venn said.

The eyes moved from the window to her face, recognized her, and were not there. Then they moved back to the moors, where the warm air carried the beginning of honey, the same air the lady had walked through three hours out and three hours back the day before, and had come home carrying.

Mrs. Venn did not raise the alarm. A house runs a long time on its own clock, and Blackmoor Hall ran: the grooms saw that the lady did not come down; the maids carried trays up and carried them down again, the broth barely tasted; and the scullery girl crossed herself at the foot of the east stair. Mrs. Venn did not stop her. It was as good a word as any for what had happened.

The summer wore on. The heather came into its full violent purple and lay over the moors like a second sea, a tide that did not move, and the lady watched it from her bed, and Mrs. Venn watched the lady, and nothing in the house changed except the direction of the light.

The lady ate what was put to her lips. She did not refuse; refusal would have required a will, and the will had been spent on the walk. She took the broth the way she had taken everything the household required of her, without argument, without desire. Mrs. Venn thought a woman could live a long time on broth and compliance if the body were willing. But the body was not willing. It was not fighting. That was what frightened Mrs. Venn most, though she could not have said why: the body was agreeing, the way the tide agrees to the moon, the way the heather agrees to the frost. There had never been any struggle in it, not since the lady had come back from the sea with her face at peace.

Below stairs the whispers ran like water. The first mistress had smiled and laughed, and look what came of it; the second had wept in private; but this one had done neither, and the scullery girl would not go up the east stair alone. The footman had said of her in the summer that she was not dying—she was being drawn, the way a needle is drawn to the pole, only no one could see the hand holding the magnet. He did not say it now. There was no need. Mrs. Venn silenced what she could and let the rest be; there was truth in it, and the truth did not need repeating.

Once, in the yellowing of the leaves, the lady spoke. Mrs. Venn was turning the lamp down and thought at first the words were for her, but they were not. They were low and even, a list, as if she were reading from a page learned long ago: Coldwell. Blackwater. Saltcombe. Rook's Reach. Then other names, names that were on no map, names that sounded like a door being built in the air.

Mrs. Venn stood very still and did not interrupt. When the list ended, she asked, "Is there anywhere you wish to be sent, my lady?"

"Home," the lady said. But her face was turned to the window, and Mrs. Venn understood that she did not mean Blackmoor Hall.

The physicians came in the autumn, from Marney and then from the county town, when the heather had gone black and the wind off the moors had turned bitter. They stood at the bedside taking the lady's pulse, looking at her tongue, asking questions she answered slowly or did not answer at all, and conferred in the corridor in the pinched voices of men who do not like to be mistaken.

"There is no fever, my lord. No obstruction we can find."

"She is not wasted in the manner of a consumption. The lungs are clear."

"I am paying you for a cause," Lord Vexford said.

"The cause, my lord, is not a disease. There are illnesses of the constitution that present no physical sign."

"She will not eat."

"She takes food when it is given to her. She does not ask for it. That is not the same thing."

"The body, my lord," the younger physician said, "can choose to lay down the burden."

Lord Vexford was a man who kept accounts, and the account of his wife would not balance. He stood in the doorway in the gray November light and looked at the woman he had married and could not find the sum he had been promised. He had married quiet, obedience, a manager for his house; he had known something was shut in her and had thought it would open, or at least would not refuse to run. It had not refused. It had run so well that the house no longer appeared to need him. This was beyond his ledger, and for the first time in their marriage it made him afraid.

He came to her bedside to say it. "You are my wife. I have summoned the best physicians in the county. Tell me what you want, and it will be brought."

The lady looked at him with eyes that recognized him and did not hold him. "Let the window stand open to the east," she said.

It was not what he had meant, and he knew it, and he stood there recognizing that it was the only thing she had said to him since the altar that was not a door. He gave the order. He left for Marney before the first snow, and Mrs. Venn saw the carriage go and did not think less of him for it. A man who cannot balance an account will always seek a sum he understands. The lamp burned in the study window through the dark, though no one was on the road to see.

The winter came down like the closing of a door. Snow made a white sea of the moors; the east staircase frosted on the inside; and the lady lay with her face turned toward the window, watching the only direction that mattered. The pale ring on her wrist had faded until it was the color of her skin, a ghost of a ring, visible only to someone who knew to look. Mrs. Venn knew to look. She looked every morning when she came with the broth.

The wedding ring had always been too large for her finger; one morning it lay on the coverlet, where it had slipped off in the night, and Mrs. Venn worked it back over the bone and did not know why the sight of it made her want to look away. It was the only ring the lady wore now. The pale mark on her wrist was not a ring at all, only the memory of one.

In deep winter a letter came from Thornwood, in Lady Margaret's hand. Mrs. Venn read it aloud because the lady no longer asked for what was given. Lord Ashworth was dead of an apoplexy, seized in his study in the cold weather, dead before the physician could be roused. The funeral had been quiet. The county said Thornwood had grown very quiet, and Lady Margaret added that she supposed the quiet agreed with her.

The lady did not weep. She lay looking at the white sea of the moors, and after a long time she said one thing, in a voice so flat it was scarcely a voice: "The coat is empty."

Mrs. Venn did not know what the words meant. She saw the lady's hand move to her throat, to the ribbon beneath her shift, the way a sleeper touches a bruise, and then fall back. Whatever the small bright key was to, it had outlived its lock. The lady had worn it every day since the wedding, hidden against her sternum, and she wore it still. She had never tried it in any door, so far as Mrs. Venn knew; she had worn it as a vote about doors, and now there were no doors left at Thornwood to vote on. She did not remove it. There was nothing in her left to remove anything with.

Once, in the worst of the cold, Mrs. Venn climbed to the east tower. The chair stood where the lady had left it, facing the rippled window, and a film of dust lay over everything like the silence in a chapel. She had wondered all year what the lady saw from here. Nothing came from the east but the sea. The lady had spent a year watching nothing come, the way a lighthouse keeper waits for a ship that has already gone down. Mrs. Venn drew the curtain and did not climb again; the window was for the lady, and the sea was for whatever it was that never came back.

The lamp in the study burned out some night in the worst of the cold, and Mrs. Venn did not relight it. There was no one on the road to see. The seventh, nineteenth, and twenty-fourth treads of the back stair had never creaked for the lady; in the deep months of that winter they creaked for Mrs. Venn alone, and the house felt her weight, which was the weight of one who had never learned to be ghost.

The spring came late. The snow went off the moors in slow gray patches; the larks came back; and the heather, under the new green, began to stir. Day after day the purple came up through the land like a tide moving under shallows, and Mrs. Venn understood what the lady had been waiting for, the way a locked door knows its key. Not death. Death had never been the door. She was waiting for the season to turn again, for the green to come back to the moors and the heather to follow it; and when it came, it would be all.

One morning she asked to be lifted. Mrs. Venn lifted her—she weighed nothing, a bird's weight, a child's—and settled her in the chair by the window with a shawl over her knees. The lady looked at the moors for a long time, at the green coming up through the gray, and Mrs. Venn stood behind her with her hands folded and did not speak. After a while the lady said, "It is beginning." Mrs. Venn, watching the first of the heather breaking open along the churchyard wall, said only, "Yes, my lady. It is."

She asked to be lifted once more, the next morning. That night Mrs. Venn sat with her through the dark. The lady's breath came slow and even, and once, near dawn, without opening her eyes, she said something Mrs. Venn did not quite catch—"wearing…," or perhaps it was "winter," or perhaps nothing at all, a word going into the pillow like a thread pulled through cloth. Mrs. Venn leaned closer, but the lady was asleep again, or past sleeping, and the breath moved in her and out of her like a tide that had almost gone out.

She died quietly that morning, at the turn of the year's long days, when the first heather was breaking open across the moors. Her face was turned to the east window, which stood open at her asking, and the morning light moved over her like water. There had been no struggle, no cry, no last effort of the breath to mark the passage except the stopping of it. She had counted the lashes once, and the heartbeats on the ride home, and the cracks in the ceiling through a year of dawns; what was left was only the last count, and it was very small, and it finished.

Mrs. Venn found her with the broth untouched and the gray gown folded, and she closed the lady's eyes with her own hand because there was no one else to do it, and the house stood silent around them, a clock that had run down.

She felt no alarm. She had watched the lady leaving for a year; the leaving had completed itself. What she felt was closer to recognition. The lady had not died of grief—grief passes. She had not died of love. She had died of the keeping: of carrying the sea inside her until there was no room left for the ordinary tide of breath. It is a kind of death, Mrs. Venn thought, standing in the finished room, for a woman to give everything she has, and to be, at the last, understood.

The body was carried down the back stair, and Mrs. Venn noticed that the seventh, nineteenth, and twenty-fourth treads creaked now, under the weight of the men who bore her. The house had accepted her as a ghost, silent on the boards, all those months; it did not know what to do with the dead. They took her out through the service door, the way she had come, and the carriage began the long slow journey back to Thornwood—the only journey she had made home since the wedding morning, past the fold of the land and the broken gate and the shallow valley she had walked to the sea and walked back from, past the shepherd's hut whose roof had fallen in.

A shepherd on the high ground watched the funeral from far off and told his wife that the grave was in the right place, for he had seen the lady walking the moors before her death, walking east with her face to the sea, and the moors had let her pass like one of their own. The story added itself to the other stories, the way water finds the low ground.

The county heard, and told the story as it told all her story: the walking ghost of Blackmoor Hall had finished walking, and the heather was blooming as they buried her. They buried her in the Ashworth family plot, in the green earth beside her father, who had died of the apoplexy the previous winter. Lord Vexford stood at the grave with his hat in his hand and his face unreadable, a man whose account had finally closed. Lady Margaret wept with the terrible efficiency of a woman who weeps for many things and names none of them. The servants of Thornwood stood at the far edge of the churchyard; Bess wept without sound, and Martha did not come to the grave, and no one sent for her. The wind came up off the moors and took the words of the blessing and scattered them over the heather. A stone was set over the grave, and a lettering chosen, and the heather came up around it before the year was out.

The heather was beginning to bloom. It came through the new green, a purple so deep it read as black in the low light, and it spread over the moors the way the sea moves under the cliffs at Raven's Point, patient and violent at once. The wind combed it, and the grave was green, and then it was the color of all the rest of the land, because that is the mercy of the heather: it covers everything. It does not choose. It blooms over the buried and the unburied alike, over the lord seized in his study and the daughter who lay down with her face to the window, over the river that was crossed and the cliff that was not, over the sea that is still the last door left open. It held their memory the way the sea holds a river—taken in, carried, invisible, and still there.

chapters.name: The Moors Still Walk Her
chapters.content:
The stone was plain, as the house had been plain, and the name upon it was cut in letters the weather would soften before a generation had passed: ELARA ASHWORTH VEXFORD, OF THORNWOOD AND BLACKMOOR HALL, born at the year's turn, dead at the year's turn, nineteen years of age and then some months. Beneath the dates a stonecutter had set the line the county would carry longer than it carried the name:

SHE WALKS THE MOORS STILL.

The words had come to the stonecutter in the black cold of the funeral time, on good paper, in a firm plain hand, with the fee paid in advance and no name at the foot of the page. The stonecutter was a precise man who had cut the names of half the county's dead and had learned that grief made people strange and that the strange requests of the grief-stricken were best executed without comment. Still, he had looked at the line for a long while, the chisel cold in his hand, and asked the messenger whether he was to cut the words as they stood. The messenger, a groom from Blackmoor Hall who had been told not to linger and not to answer questions, said he was. The stonecutter cut. He was a man of exact execution and no curiosity, and if he ever knew more, he spent it the way the moors spend their dead, which is to say he did not spend it at all.

How the words came there was argued at dinner tables through the county for a year. Some said Lady Margaret had chosen them, standing at a window of Thornwood of a moonless night with a name she never spoke. Some said Lord Vexford had ordered them like a debt paid, a man who had failed to balance the account of his second wife as he had failed to balance his first. Some said the tall housekeeper of Blackmoor Hall had written the order herself, sealing the paper with no seal and sending it by a groom who knew better than to read it, and that no one had asked twice who had authorized it, for Mrs. Venn was not a person one asked twice. But the telling the county preferred was that the words were the lady's own, spoken at the end to the only one who sat with her, and carried afterward like a candle through a dark house. Mrs. Venn kept her silence, and her silence was the kind of door that stays shut, and the legend grew around it the way the heather grew around the stone.

The legend had begun long before the burial, for the lady had been a story while she lived. Lady Pritcham of the dower house told it at every gathering she attended, and she attended all of them. She told of the bride who had come to Blackmoor Hall like a ghost and run it like a clerk, who had never smiled and never laughed, who had stood at the east-tower window with her face to the moors through a whole year of dawns. She told how she had once asked the lady whether she was happy, and the lady had answered with an inventory of the household—the soup was very good, it deserved to be taken seriously—and how Lady Pritcham had named her a walking ghost, and how the lady had looked at her with those eyes and said, *Use the phrase when you tell the story.* This last detail Lady Pritcham delivered with a shiver of self-importance, for she had been made part of the story, and she always used the phrase, and the story grew each telling.

In the telling, the details altered the way the heather alters the contours of a hill, imperceptibly and then entirely. The black hair became hair the color of the moors in winter. The single flat answer to the question of happiness became a silence that had lasted three minutes by Lady Pritcham's own timepiece. The lady's thinness, which the physicians had noted and failed to explain, became a wasting that had begun on her wedding day and had never once relented. The east-tower window, which the lady had watched the moors through, became a window she had been watching the sea through, and the sea, in Lady Pritcham's telling, had been waiting for her all along.

The county added the rest as water finds the low ground. It learned that the lady had walked to Raven's Point on the anniversary of the servant's death, walked there alone through the heather and come back changed; that she had asked that her windows stand open to the east; that she had lain down to die as quietly as a lamp reaching the end of its tallow. It learned that Lord Ashworth had died in his study in the cold winter, and that his daughter was buried beside him in the green earth, and that the heather had come up around the grave before the year was out. What the county did not learn—what no one learned—was the whole of it: the hunting lodge, the stolen hours, the flogging, the flight, the cliff. The lady had kept that account herself, and she had closed the ledger when she closed her eyes. All that remained of it was the shepherd's testimony, which spread slowly over the high ground like a mist.

The shepherd was an old man who had seen the lady walking east on the anniversary, and had not hailed her, because a woman in gray crossing the moors was no more remarkable than the wind. He had stood on the ridge and watched the funeral carriage go by, and had told his wife the grave was rightly placed, for the moors had let the lady pass like one of their own. In the years after, when the story grew into the shape it would keep, he told it again at the inn in the county town. He was not a man given to embellishment. He sat by the fire with his pewter pot and told what he had seen, and because he did not embellish it, the county believed him.

"She walked to the sea," he said, in the flat voice of a man reporting the weather. "She walked back. She lies in the right ground." He drank, and the company leaned in, and a clerk from the county town asked whether he had ever seen her since. The old shepherd considered the question with the patience of a man who has watched many seasons turn. "If you want to see her," he said at last, "walk the moors at the turning of the year, when the heather is beginning. You will not see her if you look. You will see her if you do not."

The clerk laughed, uneasy, and asked what that meant, which was precisely the wrong question. The shepherd set down his pot and looked at him with pale eyes faded by weather. "It means the moors have taken her in," he said. "The way they take in the rain and the frost and the sheep that lie down and do not get up. She is in the land now. You cannot see the rain after it falls." He stood, and would not be drawn further, and the company was left to argue about whether he had meant the lady was a ghost or a story or simply a memory the land had folded into itself, like the pale ring the grass had left on her wrist that last year, invisible unless you knew to look.

And so the sightings began.

A peddler on the Marney road saw a figure in gray at dusk, far off, walking east toward the coast, and when he looked again there was only the mist lying in the fold of the land and a single bird crossing the gray sky. He told the tale at the next inn, and the tale went the way of all tales. A young woman out riding—some said Lady Pritcham's own niece—reined in on the high ground and saw a woman in gray standing beside the broken gate that leaned on a single hinge, her face turned toward the sea, and had raised her hand to hail her, and the figure was not there, only the stones and the heather moving in the wind like a skirt.

The niece, who had a reputation for a level head that she did not entirely resent, told the story differently. She had not been frightened, she said. That was the strange part. She had seen a figure at the gate and had taken it for a woman of the moor, the wife of some shepherd looking for a stray. Then the light had changed, the way it does when a cloud passes, and the figure was gone, and the heather had been moving where she had stood, and the girl had understood without being told that she had seen the lady. She did not use the word ghost, even afterward. "She was looking east," the niece said. "She was not waiting. She was going somewhere, and she was not sorry for it." This, too, went into the story, and the story was stronger for it.

A shepherd's boy, sent to bring in the ewes, came home white-faced and said he had seen a woman in gray standing at Raven's Point, at the very edge, looking down at the water, and when he blinked she was gone. His father, the old shepherd who had spoken at the inn, looked at him a long moment and said only, *Some call her the lady. Some call her the wind. All of it is true.* The boy did not sleep well for a month, but he told the story for the rest of his life, and each telling had the same strange quiet at the center, the sense that what he had seen had been looking at the sea and not waiting for anything.

Thornwood remained through it all, cold and silent, a monument to the world that had broken her. The house had always been cavernous and dark; now it was simply empty in the way a shell is empty. Lady Margaret grew old there alone, moving through the rooms with a lamp though it was not night, writing letters she did not send. She visited the grave in all weathers and left flowers the wind took, and once, standing before the stone with her veil down, she said aloud to no one, "You took after me. That was the cruel thing." She never said what she meant, and the county, which had always found something a little unaccountable in Lady Margaret, added it to the story. Some said she meant the stubbornness, the will, the way her daughter had refused to be a piece on the board her mother had spent a lifetime learning to play. Some said she meant the restless eye at the window, the girl who watched the road. But whatever she had meant, she never spoke it again, and the veil came down, and she returned to Thornwood with her lamp and her unsent letters, a widow who wept for many things and named none of them.

Bess, who had helped the lady escape on the night before the wedding, stayed on at Thornwood the way a root stays in a wall. She married Jem the stable boy, who had grown into a quiet, steady man and had never told anyone about the chalice or the man who had been brought to the gallows post. Their first daughter was dark-eyed and grave, with a way of standing at the window that made her mother's heart stop, and Bess named her Elara, and no one argued. When the child was old enough to understand, Bess told her the story as it was told in the county: the lady who walked the moors, who lay in the Ashworth plot, whose grave had heather for a blanket. She did not tell the other story, the one she carried like a stone in her pocket. That story she visited every Sunday of her life at the grave, standing silent while her husband and children spoke their prayers, and the stone had no answer for her, and she asked for none.

Martha, who had loved the man and betrayed him and believed to her death that she had been saving him, was not at the grave, and no one sent for her. She had gone to the town in the end, to lodge with a widowed sister, and was seen at the market with her basket and her silence. Twice a year she paid a boy to walk to Thornwood and look at the grave and tell her what the stone said, and the boy always told her the same words, and Martha always paid him and sent him away. She told no one the message she had carried so many years, the one she had exacted her price for—*tell him Martha let you go*—and the message died with her, as all undelivered things die, leaving only the shape of a debt no one could collect.

At Blackmoor Hall the east tower stood with its chair and its dust and its drawn curtain. The lamp in the study window was never relit, for there was no one on the road to see, and Mrs. Venn, growing old in the service of a house that no longer required her vigilance, kept the lady's rooms as the lady had left them. The seventh, nineteenth, and twenty-fourth treads of the back stair creaked now under her weight alone, for she had never learned to be a ghost, and the house felt her. Young maids whispered that the east tower was haunted, and Mrs. Venn told them it was not haunted, it was merely waiting, and that there were worse things to be. Lord Vexford was said to be considering the widow in Marney's town, whose auburn hair and low warm laugh had been seen at his table; it was also said he would not marry again, for the account of his second wife had never closed to his satisfaction, and a man who cannot balance a sum will not reopen the books. Whatever the truth, the moss-green handkerchief remained in his laundry, and no one in the house asked whose it was.

The years passed, as they will, and the heather covered everything, the buried and the unburied alike, for that is the mercy of the heather. It bloomed over the grave in the Ashworth plot, over the cliff where no grave was, over the river that had been crossed and the river that had not. The wind came off the sea and moved across the moors in long gray strokes, and there were those who said that if you listened you could hear two names in it, or one name spoken twice, or only the sound of the wind, which is perhaps the truest telling.

Travelers crossing the moors at the turn of the year still see her sometimes—a woman in gray walking east toward Raven's Point, her face turned toward the sea, walking with the unhurried gait of one who is not going anywhere she has not already been. Those who call out find nothing but heather and the shadow of a cloud. Those who do not call out walk on, and the story walks with them, and the moors hold the memory of two lovers the way the sea holds a river—taken in, carried, invisible, and still there, in the sound of the wind and the blooming of the heather over their sorrow, and the stone that says, in letters the weather is slowly softening, *She walks the moors still.*
